Abstract

Differential emission measure (DEM) inversion finds how much coronal plasma lies at each temperature along a line of sight, one optimisation per pixel. Supervised emulators need solver DEMs for every training image. We train on the solver's objective instead: an MLP maps one pixel's six SDO/AIA intensities to the solver's 54 basis weights, trained on Basis Pursuit's (BP) sparsity and noise-band objective or on ElasticNet's; solver DEMs only score it. The final BP model has 1.5M parameters, the ElasticNet model 409k. On 153 held-out images (86 distinct days) the ElasticNet model beats a supervised emulator on every measure (DEM MSE 0.310 against 0.318). The BP model wins four of six headline measures with a median pixel error 3.6 times lower (0.031 against 0.112); its DEM MSE is 1.2 times higher (1.08 against 0.91), and flare cores, one pixel in 10,000, hold 92% of its squared error. BP's original failure there was the loss, not training: at band weight μ = 1 the quadratic exterior penalty prices hot plasma out. A stiffer band (μ = 100) restores it (flare-core emission 40% to 96.7% of the solver's). Penalty-method theory gives the band violation as λ_c tσ_c/(2μ), so μ follows from the response, the noise and a tolerance. Larger models blow up on scores only when trained without deconvolution-clamp pixels; with them a 1.5M model is the best BP model. Small models lose from those pixels (BP 409k 2.37 to 2.79, ElasticNet 409k 0.310 to 0.439), so the ElasticNet final excludes them.

1. Introduction

The differential emission measure (DEM) says how much plasma lies at each temperature along a line of sight. It is a key diagnostic of coronal thermal structure, separating the warm corona near 1 MK (logT 6.0) from flare plasma near 8 MK (logT 6.9). The Atmospheric Imaging Assembly (AIA; Lemen et al. 2012) on the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO) images the full disk at 4096 × 4096 pixels in six EUV channels (94, 131, 171, 193, 211 and 335 Å), each sensitive to a different mix of temperatures, so a DEM can be estimated for every pixel of every image.

Six intensities constrain a DEM on 18 temperature bins, so many DEMs fit the observations within their noise, and the solver's tie-break decides the shape it reports (section 2). Two solvers are the references here. Basis Pursuit (BP) returns the DEM with the smallest total basis weight that reproduces every channel within a noise band, one linear program per pixel. ElasticNet fits the same basis by least squares with L1 and L2 penalties on the weights. BP follows Cheung et al. (2015) and the ElasticNet form Athiray and Winebarger (2024); DeepEM (Wright et al. 2019) first trained a network on BP's DEMs.

Both solve every pixel separately, which is what makes them expensive. One image on our 2048 × 2048 grid (every second AIA pixel in each direction) is 4.2 million problems. BP solved about 1,400 pixels per second per CPU core; with the deconvolution and the retries at relaxed tolerances, a BP job took about 9.5 minutes per image on 16 cores and an ElasticNet job about 5.25. Clean BP and ElasticNet DEMs for our 1,223 images took 2,446 such jobs and 1.74 TB of output.

Supervised emulators move this cost into training. DeepEM trained a network on solver DEMs, and the supervised side's emulator modernises it with Fourier-feature inputs, a wider SiLU network and a binned distribution over each output. Inference is one forward pass per pixel, but the model stays bound to its labels. It needs solver DEMs for every training image. A change of solver settings invalidates them: 886 GB of our first ElasticNet DEMs (α = 1) were superseded when the supervised side's α = 0.001 was confirmed. And it learns the solver's answer even where that answer is questionable: at the 40% of pixels where the deconvolution clamped a channel to zero, nearly all faint, BP still fits a DEM to the artefact (section 7.2).

We instead train on the solver's objective, which depends only on the observations and their noise. This is amortised optimisation: one network learns the map from an observation to its solution instead of solving each pixel afresh, and it never sees a solver DEM. The objective must be the solver's own: in an early per-pixel test, losses that only fit the six channels reproduced AIA about 12 times better than BP yet landed about 5 times further from its DEMs (appendix A). The network reads one pixel's six intensities and outputs the solvers' 54 basis weights, from which the fixed basis and response matrix give the DEM and the predicted intensities. For ElasticNet the loss is the solver's objective with its settings; for BP it is the sparsity term with the band as a penalty, zero inside and quadratic outside, weighted by the band weight μ (section 3). When the ElasticNet setting changed, the model was simply retrained. Solver DEMs enter only the evaluation, on the supervised side's protocol: both models are scored on the same pixels of 153 test images (86 distinct days, September to December 2015) against the same solver DEMs (section 4); ours trains on 917 earlier images. The work is AIA-only; XRT and the uncertainty output are left open, and the network's speed against the solver is unmeasured (section 9).

This report makes four claims.

  1. Label-free training matches or beats a supervised emulator. Our final models are per-pixel MLPs on one pixel's six intensities, trained only on the solver's objective: 409k parameters on ElasticNet, 1.5M on BP. The first is ahead of the supervised model on every measure. The second is ahead on four of six headline measures and 3.6 times closer to BP on the typical pixel (median pixel error 0.031 against 0.112), and loses DEM MSE (1.08 against 0.91) and AIA MAE (section 5).
  2. The one BP failure was in the loss. At flare cores the network sat close to its loss's per-pixel optimum (a median 8% above it), and at μ = 1 that optimum leaves out the hot plasma. A stiffer band (μ = 100) puts it back: flare-core emission rises from 40% of the solver's to 93% with a 409k model and 96.7% with the final one (section 6). μ need not be tuned blind: penalty-method theory places each channel λ_c tσ_c / (2μ) half-widths outside its band at the optimum, with λ_c the channel's dual price in BP's linear program, so μ follows from the response matrix, the noise and a chosen tolerance (section 3.3).
  3. Larger models blow up on scores only when trained without the clamp pixels. At scale the per-pixel MLP beats the patch CNN, and larger MLPs improve the typical pixel a little (section 5.4). Trained without the pixels where the deconvolution clamped a channel to zero, they blow up on a few rare pixels: inputs that training excluded, lone single-channel spikes among zeroed channels, where a larger network extrapolates further (section 7.1). With those pixels kept and only the clamped channels freed from the band, a 1.5M model drops from DEM MSE 897 to 1.08 and is the best BP model we have. The small models lose from the same change (BP 409k 2.37 to 2.79 at 40 epochs, ElasticNet 409k 0.310 to 0.439), so the ElasticNet final stays at 409k without them. A few single-channel outliers remain, nearly all without a solver DEM, and a self-check on the reconstruction flags them (section 7.1).
  4. The remaining error is concentrated. Flare cores, where some channel reaches 32 times its Bright cutoff, are one pixel in 10,000 yet hold 92% of the final BP model's squared error and 90% of the supervised model's (section 5.2). The outliers at the low end of the AIA joint distributions are the clamp again: where a channel was zeroed the observation itself is wrong, and the solver's DEM disagrees with it too. With the clamped channels freed that low cluster holds about 5.5M pixels, 0.8% of the test set, and barely moves the scores (section 7.2).

Sections 2 to 4 give the problem, method and evaluation, sections 5 to 8 the results and their analysis, and section 9 the limitations.

2. Problem setting

2.1 Observations and the DEM

The data are SDO/AIA images in six EUV channels (94, 131, 171, 193, 211 and 335 Å), deconvolved for the instrument's point-spread function (with the revised functions of Hofmeister et al. 2025) and corrected for exposure time and degradation, so a pixel's six values o_c are intensities in DN/s. DEMs are computed on a 2048 × 2048 grid, DEM pixel (i, j) taking the AIA values at pixel (2i, 2j).

A DEM has 18 values, on temperature bins from logT 5.5 to 7.2 in steps of 0.1 dex (about 0.3 to 16 MK). Each is the emission measure in its bin in units of 10^26 cm^-5, which this report calls one unit of plasma. (The solver files pad the grid to logT 8.0 with zeros.) The response matrix R (6 × 18) gives each channel's DN/s per unit of plasma in each bin, so the predicted intensities are R times the DEM. With six measurements and 18 unknowns, many DEMs fit within the noise; the solver's regulariser picks one.

2.2 The basis

Neither solver solves for the 18 bins directly. Both solve for 54 non-negative weights w on a fixed basis B (18 × 54), with DEM = Bw and predicted intensities RBw. At each bin B has a spike (one unit in that bin and nothing elsewhere) and two Gaussians in logT centred on the bin, exp(−(ΔlogT/a)²) with a = 0.1 and 0.2 dex and a peak of 1, values below 0.04 of the peak set to zero (Table 2.1).

Table 2.1. The three basis components at a bin away from the ends of the grid.

Component Bins covered Plasma per unit of weight
Spike 1 1
Gaussian, a = 0.1 dex 3 1.74 = 1 + 2 × 0.368
Gaussian, a = 0.2 dex 7 3.50 = 1 + 2 × (0.779 + 0.368 + 0.105)

The weights are therefore not the plasma. A unit of weight on a spike is one unit of plasma in one bin, but a unit on the 0.1 dex Gaussian spreads 1.74 units over three bins, and a unit on the 0.2 dex Gaussian 3.5 units over seven. So the sum of the 54 weights, which BP minimises (our BP loss's sparsity term), is not the plasma summed over the 18 bins: a DEM shaped like one 0.2 dex Gaussian costs 1 written as that Gaussian and 3.5 written as seven spikes. Responses differ the same way: per unit of weight, the 0.2 dex Gaussian at logT 6.8 gives 94 Å 0.67 DN/s, the spike at logT 6.9 only 0.266.

Our network's basis has this truncation; the solver runs that made the reference DEMs used --notrunc, which keeps the tails, so their Gaussians carry about 1.77 and 3.54 units per unit of weight. Both generation commands we have pass --notrunc (ours for BP, the supervised side's for ElasticNet). The difference is at most 2.1% of an element's emission and moves the price bounds of section 3.3 by under 1%; where solver DEMs are rewritten as 54 weights (sections 6.3 and 8.3) the decomposition uses our truncated basis.

2.3 Noise

Each pixel and channel has a noise σ_c from AIA's instrument noise model: the estimate_error routine of aiapy (Barnes et al. 2020) with the SolarSoft error table, which adds shot (photon), dark, read, quantisation and onboard-compression noise in quadrature, with the photometric-calibration and atomic-data terms off. Shot noise grows as the square root of the counts, so the relative noise falls as a pixel brightens. In the median pixel σ/o is 1.12 in 94 Å, 0.60 in 335 Å and 0.44 in 131 Å, against 0.06 to 0.08 in 171, 193 and 211 Å. The band of channel c is o_c ± tσ_c with t = 1.4.

2.4 Basis Pursuit

For each pixel BP solves the linear program

minimise Σ_k w_k over w ≥ 0, subject to o_c − tσ_c ≤ (RBw)_c ≤ o_c + tσ_c for every channel c.

The band is a rule: every DEM inside it is equally acceptable, and the smallest weight sum breaks the tie. As a pixel brightens, its band narrows relative to the signal until it is tighter than the accuracy of R itself and no DEM fits. The solver then retries the pixel with the band three and then five times wider (t = 4.2, then 7.0) and our copy of the solver records the outcome per pixel as tolLevel: 1 inside the band, 3 or 5 after relaxation, 0 if no DEM was found. On one full-disk image, 89.78% of pixels were solved inside the band, 10.04% at three times its width, 0.16% at five times and 0.02% not at all; relaxation was more common on the disk (13.4% against 6.3% off the limb) and in brighter pixels. Section 7.3 returns to these pixels.

2.5 ElasticNet

ElasticNet fits the same weights by penalised least squares:

minimise over w ≥ 0: (1/2C) Σ_c [((RBw)_c − o_c) / (tσ_c)]² + αλ Σ_k w_k + ½α(1 − λ) Σ_k w_k²,

with each residual divided by the band's half-width tσ_c (floored at 0.5 DN/s). The supervised side's settings are α = 0.001, λ = 0.5 (the l1_ratio of scikit-learn; Pedregosa et al. 2011) and C = 6, the number of channels, since scikit-learn's ElasticNet divides the squared error by twice the number of rows; the fit is non-negative (positive=True), without intercept, with at most 10,000 iterations. With no band there is no relaxation: every pixel gets a DEM, though our solver runs at these settings logged convergence warnings. The L2 term spreads weight over more components, so ElasticNet DEMs are broader than BP's. Our first ElasticNet runs used α = 1, the code's default; every ElasticNet number in this report uses α = 0.001.

2.6 What the channels see

Table 2.2. AIA response to one unit of plasma (10^26 cm^-5) in a single bin, in DN/s.

Plasma at 94 Å 131 Å 171 Å 193 Å 211 Å 335 Å
1 to 1.3 MK (warm, logT 6.0 to 6.1) 0.19 to 0.22 0.5 to 1.2 36 to 95 29 to 55 5 to 7 0.4
8 MK (hot, logT 6.9) 0.27 0.40 0.05 0.34 0.08 0.05

A unit of warm plasma lights 171 and 193 Å by tens of DN/s and 211 Å by several, so those low-noise channels pin it down. A unit of hot plasma lights no channel by more than 0.4 DN/s. At ordinary pixels most of the 94 Å signal comes from warm plasma that the other channels demand anyway. At flare cores most of it comes from hot plasma, which only 94 and 131 Å ask for, two of the three noisiest channels, so a bright 94 Å reading needs hundreds of units of it. How a loss prices those units decides whether the hot plasma appears in the DEM at all (section 6).

3. Method: amortised optimisation

Both solvers solve one problem per pixel: from the six intensities o and their noise σ, find the 54 non-negative basis weights w that minimise the solver's objective. We train one network f_θ to do this for any pixel, by minimising the same objective over the training pixels:

$$ \theta^\star = \arg\min_\theta \sum_{p} L\left(f_\theta(o_p);\ o_p, \sigma_p\right) $$

Solving is paid for once, in training, and each new pixel then costs one forward pass. No solver DEM enters training. Solver DEMs score the result (section 4) and compare losses with different band weights on validation pixels (section 3.5).

3.1 Network

The network sees the six intensities of one pixel: not its neighbours (section 5.4) and not σ, which only the loss uses. Each intensity, in DN/s, is square-rooted and lifted to sines and cosines at 12 fixed frequencies 2π·2^(i/2), i = −4, …, 7 (Fourier features; Tancik et al. 2020), which with the square roots themselves gives 6 × 25 = 150 inputs. This is the supervised model's input path; the square root spreads the bright end far more than the old model's log1p (a 10^4 DN/s flare core maps to 100, against 9.2).

Four hidden layers with SiLU activations feed a linear layer to 54 outputs and a softplus, which keeps every weight non-negative. The softplus input is clamped at −20 so that its gradient never vanishes, and the output layer starts small (weights scaled by 0.01, bias −3) so that the first DEM reproduces intensities of the order of the observations; both fixes date from the collapse of the first full-disk runs (appendix A). The width differs by track. The final BP model is 680 wide, with 1,528,694 parameters, quoted as 1.5M; the ElasticNet model is 336 wide, with 408,630 parameters, quoted as 409k. For width W the count is 150W + 3W² + 54W weights and 4W + 54 biases. On six log1p inputs the same widths have 1.43M and 360k. Section 3.5 says how each width was set. The speed of either network against the solver has not been measured.

The output is the solver's own variable. Neither solver works on the 18 DEM bins (logT 5.5 to 7.2, 0.1 dex apart) directly: both solve for 54 weights on a fixed basis B, at each bin a spike and two Gaussians exp(−ΔlogT²/a²) with a = 0.1 and 0.2 dex, and report DEM = Bw, whose intensities are Dw with D = RB (R in DN/s per 10^26 cm^-5). Predicting the same weights, the network searches the solver's space of DEMs (the solver fits flare cores in it, so the basis is not the limit), BP's sparsity term means the same thing for both, and the sparsity score (Σw)²/Σw² is comparable with the solver's (1.79 on BP). The supervised model instead outputs the 18 bins. One difference remains: our basis zeroes each Gaussian below 0.04 of its peak, while the solver runs pass --notrunc and keep those tails, at most 2.1% of an element's emission; both generation commands we have pass it, and the difference moves the price bounds of section 3.3 by under 1%.

3.2 Losses

With o_c and σ_c the observation and noise of channel c in DN/s, (Dw)_c the intensity the DEM reproduces and t = 1.4 the solver's first tolerance level, the band is o_c ± tσ_c. The BP loss is

$$ L_{\mathrm{BP}}(w) = \sum_{k=1}^{54} w_k + \mu \sum_{c=1}^{6} \left[ \frac{\max\left(0,\ |(Dw)_c - o_c| - t\sigma_c\right)}{t\sigma_c} \right]^2, \qquad w \ge 0. $$

The first term is BP's objective, the total weight. The hinge is zero inside the band, so there is no fit term there: any DEM within the noise is equally good and sparsity breaks the tie, as in BP. Dividing by the half-width tσ_c makes a half-width outside cost the same in every channel, so 94 Å at a few DN/s counts as much as 171 Å at hundreds. The square is our choice (BP is a linear program with a hard band): it makes the penalty smooth at the edge, at the cost of an optimum that sits slightly outside the band at any finite μ (section 3.3). The band weight μ is the exchange rate between squared half-widths and units of weight. BP treats the band as a rule and the loss treats it as a price; section 6 turns on that difference. The old model used μ = 1, the final BP model the stiff band, μ = 100. Per pixel the loss is convex in w, so each pixel has one best answer under the loss.

The ElasticNet loss is

$$ L_{\mathrm{EN}}(w) = \frac{1}{2C} \sum_{c=1}^{6} \left[ \frac{(Dw)c - o_c}{t\sigma_c} \right]^2 + \alpha\lambda \sum w_k^2, \qquad w \ge 0, $$}^{54} w_k + \frac{\alpha(1-\lambda)}{2} \sum_{k=1}^{54

with the supervised side's α = 0.001, λ = 0.5 and C = 6. This is the solver's objective term for term (scikit-learn's non-negative ElasticNet fitted to D and o divided by tσ_c, whose 1/(2N) over N = 6 rows is the 1/(2C) above), except that the solver floors tσ_c at 0.5 DN/s; on the staged validation errors 1.4σ falls below 0.5 DN/s at under 0.1% of pixels, so the floor hardly ever binds. The L2 term makes it strictly convex, so each pixel's best answer under the loss is, up to that floor, the solver's DEM; and with no band there is nothing to price, which is why ElasticNet never had BP's flare-core failure. Both losses are averaged over the 8,192 pixels of a batch.

3.3 The band weight μ

The BP loss is the quadratic exterior penalty of BP's linear program,

$$ \min_{w \ge 0} \ \sum_{k} w_k \quad \text{subject to} \quad o_c - t\sigma_c \le (Dw)_c \le o_c + t\sigma_c, \quad c = 1, \dots, 6, $$

and penalty-method theory says what it does at finite μ (Nocedal and Wright 2006, chapter 17). At the penalised optimum, a channel whose band edge binds sits outside the band by v_c DN/s, where the marginal penalty, 2μv_c/(tσ_c)² per DN/s, equals the marginal saving in total weight: the linear program's dual price λ_c of that edge, in weight units per DN/s. Hence

$$ \frac{2\mu\, v_c}{(t\sigma_c)^2} = \lambda_c \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad \frac{v_c}{t\sigma_c} = \frac{\lambda_c\, t\sigma_c}{2\mu}. $$

In half band-widths the violation falls as 1/μ and grows with the noise and the price. The relation is exact once μ is large enough that the penalised optimum keeps the basis elements and binding edges of the linear program's solution.

When a single edge binds, the linear program can always buy a DN/s of that channel from its most efficient basis element, so R and B alone bound the price:

$$ \lambda_c \le \frac{1}{\max_k \, (RB)_{c,k}}. $$

Table 3.1. Single-channel price bound, in weight units (10^26 cm^-5) per DN/s.

94 Å 131 Å 171 Å 193 Å 211 Å 335 Å
1.48 0.10 0.003 0.007 0.026 0.60

The bound differs more than 400-fold between 94 Å and 171 Å: a unit of weight buys at most two thirds of a DN/s of 94 Å but a few hundred of 171 Å. 94 Å is the dear channel.

At the flare core worked through in section 6, 94 Å reads 164 DN/s with σ = 11.5, so tσ = 16.1 and the band runs from 148 to 180. At the bound the 94 Å violation is 1.48 × 16.1/(2μ) = 11.9/μ half-widths. At μ = 1 that exceeds the 9.2 half-widths (148/16.1) by which a DEM without hot plasma falls short, so the best answer drops the hot plasma outright. At μ = 10 the violation is 1.19 half-widths, at 30 it is 0.40, at 100 0.12 and at 300 0.04; μ = 120 holds the pixel within 0.1 half-width.

Turned round, a tolerance of ε half-widths needs μ ≥ λ_c tσ_c/(2ε), a number set by the response, the basis and the noise, with no solver DEM. Photon noise makes σ grow as the square root of the counts, so the μ needed grows with the square root of the brightness. Faint pixels have small σ, and their 94 Å comes free with the warm plasma that 171, 193 and 211 Å demand (section 6), so they hardly respond to μ; flare cores combine the largest σ with the dearest channel and need μ near 100. The same law, a small violation below the lower band edges that shrinks as 1/μ, explains the old model's emission deficit at ordinary pixels: on validation pixels at 0.3 to 1 times the Bright cutoff, the best answer under the loss emits 0.861 of the solver's emission at μ = 1 and 1.009 at μ = 100.

Two refinements follow, neither yet trained. A per-pixel, per-channel weight proportional to λ_c tσ_c, with the bound standing in for λ_c, needs only R, B and σ and would hold every pixel to the same tolerance. An L1 exterior penalty, μ Σ_c max(0, |(Dw)_c − o_c| − tσ_c)/(tσ_c), is exact: once μ exceeds λ_c tσ_c in every binding channel (about 24 at the flare core above), its minimiser solves BP's linear program itself, at the cost of a slope that jumps at the band edge.

The bound assumes one binding edge. When several bind, the price can exceed it, because the element that sets the bound may push another channel out of its band. The 94 Å bound comes from warm plasma, the 0.2 dex Gaussian at logT 6.1 (0.676 DN/s per unit), which also lights 171 Å; at a flare core the hot element at logT 6.8 (0.669 DN/s per unit) sets a price 1% higher, and other combinations can raise it further. The theory is therefore checked on validation pixels.

Validation check. On the 11,954 validation pixels of the μ screen (every flare core of the split and about 1,000 per brightness band), we solved BP's linear program at t = 1.4 for its dual prices and the best answer under the loss at μ = 1 to 1,000, and compared the measured violation with λ_c tσ_c/(2μ) (experiments/mu_theory.py, Figure 3.2).

  • The law holds. At μ = 100 the measured violation divided by the predicted one has a median of 1.00 over 45,925 violated pixel-channels, and the median is 1.00 in every brightness band for μ ≥ 10. μ times the violation stays constant from μ = 10 to 1,000 (a coefficient of variation of 0.00 to 0.06 at the median pixel below flare cores, 0.19 at flare cores). Below μ ≈ 10 the best answer drops basis elements the linear program keeps, the hot plasma at bright pixels, and the first-order law no longer applies (at flare cores the median ratio is 0.66 at μ = 1).
  • The prices. At flare cores the median 94 Å price is 1.46, at the single-edge bound of 1.48; it exceeds the bound at 49% of them (99th percentile 8.8) where other edges bind. 94 Å is the dearest channel at 70% of flare cores, 335 Å at 15% and 131 Å at 13%; over all pixels 94 Å leads at 40%, 335 Å at 26% and 131 Å at 17%.
  • μ for a tolerance. From the measured prices, holding the median flare core within 0.5, 0.2 and 0.1 half-widths needs μ = 34, 84 and 168; the 90th-percentile flare core needs 153, 382 and 763. At μ = 100 the median flare core sits about 0.17 half-widths outside its band and the 90th percentile about 0.8, roughly one noise σ beyond the edge. Over all pixels the median needs only μ = 13 for 0.5 and 64 for 0.1. A single global μ cannot hold every pixel to one tolerance: the most demanding feasible pixel in the sample, a flare core priced on 335 Å, would need 63,801 for 0.1 half-width. This is the case for the per-pixel weight above.
  • Infeasible pixels. At 8.8% of the sample (12% of flare cores) no DEM fits the 1.4σ band, and these are exactly the pixels the solver relaxed (section 7.3). There the violation stops falling at a floor set by the observation, whatever μ, and the law does not apply.

So μ is not a free hyperparameter. Given the response, the basis and the noise, the theory states how far outside its band the best answer sits at any μ, and validation confirms it pixel by pixel. μ = 100 is the value that holds the typical flare core to about a sixth of a half-width; section 7.3 shows that once the band is relaxed where the solver relaxes it, larger μ only moves the best answer closer to the solver.

3.4 Training

The 1,223 full-disk images (2014 and 2015, about two a day, deconvolved, with σ per pixel and channel; section 2) are split in time: 917 for training (1 January 2014 to 16 June 2015), 153 for validation (to 21 September 2015) and 153 for test (to 31 December 2015). Each image's 2048 by 2048 DEM grid is cut into 256 blocks of 128 by 128 pixels, of which a seeded random 64 are kept once at staging: 58,688 training blocks. AIA is subsampled by 2, so DEM pixel (i, j) sees AIA pixel (2i, 2j), the one the solver used. Each epoch draws 512 fresh pixels uniformly from the valid pixels of every block, 30,048,256 in all, off-disk pixels included.

A pixel is valid if the solver solved it (this flag, not a DEM, is the one solver output training reads) and its observations and σ are finite. The positivity clamp after deconvolution sets negative values to zero, so a channel can read zero where the others carry signal. We call a channel clamped when it reads at or below MIN_OBS = 10^-3 DN/s, three decades below the faintest channel's median (94 Å, 0.76 DN/s). A clamped channel is an artefact, and the solver fits a DEM to it anyway.

There are two treatments. The first, used for the ElasticNet model and for every BP run before the confirmation runs of section 7.1, drops every pixel with a clamped channel from training and validation. That mask was estimated at about 5% of pixels from the two brightest channels; counted over all six it drops about 40% of valid pixels (39.7% on the shared test set), nearly all faint (section 7.1). The second (--clamp_mode mask), used for the final BP model, keeps those pixels and frees only their clamped channels: such a channel's band is made so wide that it adds nothing to the loss, the other channels keep their bands, and the network still reads the zero as an input. The ElasticNet loss drops a freed channel the same way. Either way the pixels stay in the test set (section 7.2). Keeping them is what removed the large models' score blow-ups (section 7.1).

Until 2 October 2026 each block's draw was seeded by its index alone, so every epoch reused one fixed sample of 30M pixels, about 0.8% of the training images' pixels (appendix C); every full-disk model in sections 5 to 8 was trained with fresh pixels.

Training uses Adam (Kingma and Ba 2015; peak learning rate 3 × 10^-4, no weight decay) with a linear warm-up of 500 steps on BP and 3,000 on ElasticNet, then cosine decay to zero; batches of 16 blocks of 512 pixels, 3,668 steps per epoch; and a global gradient-norm clip at 1, which on the stiff band acts on every step (norms 20 to 500; without it the AIA fit improved but every DEM measure got worse). The ElasticNet model trains 40 epochs. The final BP model trains 120 epochs at μ = 100 from scratch. The earlier 409k stiff-band model (width 336, clamp pixels excluded) trained 120 epochs at μ = 100, then 120 more from that checkpoint with --init_from (weights only; new optimiser, warm-up and schedule). The full training state is saved every epoch, so runs proceed in resumable segments of under two hours, past which the cluster cancels GPU jobs at low utilisation; the model used is the last epoch's, with no early stopping. An epoch of the ElasticNet model takes 152 to 174 s on one GPU, so its 40 epochs take under two hours; the final BP model took a median 169 s per epoch and 6.6 hours in all.

3.5 Model selection on validation

For a fixed loss we select on the training loss itself, computed after every epoch on a fixed validation sample, with no solver DEM: 512 pixels from each of the first 256 validation blocks, 131,072 pixels. Blocks are stored in time order, 64 to an image, so these are the first four validation images, 16 to 18 June 2015.

This signal chose the per-pixel MLP over the patch CNN (section 5.4), width 336 on the original BP loss (2.148 against 2.155 at 1.43M, a tie that favours the smaller model) and the square root plus Fourier input on ElasticNet (0.0533 against 0.0575 for log1p); on the original BP loss the input tied (2.1472 against 2.1478), so the old model kept log1p. On the stiff band it chose the new input for BP (5.731 against 6.006), kept the clip (against 8.052 without it) and ranks the 409k stiff-band model first among the 409k stiff-band runs (5.444, against 5.488 for 240 epochs from scratch and 5.648 for 120). The screen's DEM error, below, preferred 240 epochs from scratch (14.0 against 15.8), but that run put 130 times the 120-epoch model's band penalty on the validation flare cores, against 13 times for the continuation.

Different band weights give different losses, so μ cannot be chosen on the training loss. The band weight and the stiff-band candidates were compared on about 12,000 pixels drawn from all 153 validation images, 6,000 of them flare cores, by DEM error against the solver's DEMs with each brightness band weighted by its share of pixels (section 6): the one place solver DEMs enter a choice. The screen's 94 Å column needs no solver DEM and levels off at μ = 100 (26%, 81%, 89%, 93% and 94% at μ = 1, 10, 30, 100 and 300). The band weight was chosen this way before the account of section 3.3 existed; that account now says why the screen levelled off there.

Three choices were made with test evidence, because 131k pixels from four images are too few for the rarest pixels and, with clamp pixels excluded, contain none of the inputs that fail. The first is width. At matched training the validation loss tied with or preferred every model above 409k parameters that we trained (on ElasticNet 0.0533 at 722k, 0.0528 at 1.43M and 0.0522 at 10M, against 0.0575 with the log1p input and 0.0533 with the final input at width 336; on the stiff BP band 5.562 at 1.5M and 5.706 at 10M, against 5.648 and 5.731), yet each blew up on a few rare test pixels (DEM MSE 3.24, 36.2 and 2,062 against 0.48 and 0.310 on ElasticNet; 897 and 35.7 against 2.00 and 2.37 on BP). With clamp pixels excluded, width 336 is the largest that does not blow up on either track, which is why the ElasticNet model stays at 409k; on BP the screen's stratified sample also flagged the 1.5M model (DEM error 4,170 against 17.8). The second is the ElasticNet training length: 120 epochs reaches a lower validation loss (0.0523 against 0.0533) and improves DEM MAE, the median pixel error, EM error, W1 and AIA MAE on test, but worsens DEM MSE from 0.310 to 0.362 and AIA MSE from 161 to 188, so 40 epochs stay.

The third is the final BP model itself. The validation losses of clamp-mask runs use a different mask from the earlier runs (the 1.5M run ends at 4.910 against the 409k stiff-band model's 5.444, on a sample that now holds faint clamp pixels), so they cannot rank the two, and no 409k clamp run at 120 epochs exists to compare at matched training. The 1.5M clamp model was therefore chosen on test scores: DEM MSE 1.08, against 1.75 for the 409k stiff-band model and 2.79 for the 409k clamp run at 40 epochs. μ = 100 was kept from the screen; the relaxed-band run at μ = 300 was not adopted (section 7.3). Validating on every pixel of the 153 validation images, clamp pixels included, is the fix (section 9).

4. Evaluation protocol

Both models are scored on the supervised side's protocol: the same test pixels, the same solver DEMs as targets, the same Bright cutoffs and the same validity rule, so every comparison in section 5 is made on identical pixels. Each track is scored against its own solver's DEMs.

4.1 The shared test set

The test images are the 153 of the time split, taken on 86 distinct days from 21 September to 31 December 2015. None was used in training, and they entered model selection only in the three exceptions of section 3.5. The split has no gap at this end: the first test image follows the last validation image by 47 s. Each image has five solver targets: the solve of the clean image and four re-solves of copies with Gaussian noise added of half the estimated σ (the generation command passes no --noisescale, and fullBP.py defaults it to 0.5; earlier material said σ). The noisy files store only the DEM, so the network's input is the clean AIA for all five. Each target is scored on its own seeded random 64 of the image's 256 blocks of 128 by 128 pixels, which gives 48,960 blocks and 802,160,640 pixel-targets, all of them valid on ElasticNet. On BP, 705,016,779 carry a solver DEM and the other 12% carry none. They are the pixels where no DEM fits the 1.4σ band: the generation passes --zerochill, which skips the solver's relaxation, and the missing share is 7.7% at clean solves, close to the 8.5% our own clean labels relax, and 12% to 13% at the noisier re-solves (section 7.3). Nothing else is removed: the deconvolution-clamp pixels, which the final BP model trains on and the ElasticNet model does not (section 3.4), are all scored (section 7.2).

4.2 Bright, Quiet and brightness bands

Table 4.1. Bright cutoffs, each channel's top 5% of intensities over the test split, in DN/s.

94 Å 131 Å 171 Å 193 Å 211 Å 335 Å
3.1212 16.9986 448.8948 498.3444 190.7388 10.3326

A valid pixel is Bright when any channel reaches its cutoff and Quiet otherwise; Full is all valid pixels. Bright is 10.1% of the BP pixel-targets and 10.5% of the ElasticNet ones. The cutoffs come from the test split; training uses them only to log the share of Bright pixels it draws.

The analyses by brightness use I, the largest channel over its own cutoff, in nine bands with edges at 10^-1.5, 10^-1, 10^-0.5, 1, 10^0.25, 10^0.5, 10 and 10^1.5, written 0.03, 0.1, 0.3, 1, 1.8, 3.2, 10 and 32 times the cutoff. The first four bands are Quiet and the other five Bright. Flare cores are the pixels at 32 times the cutoff and above: 69,283 BP pixel-targets (0.0098%) and 75,832 on ElasticNet (0.0095%). Table 5.4 (section 5.2) gives each band's share of pixels.

4.3 DEM measures

A pixel-target is valid when the solver's DEM is finite in all 18 bins and the prediction is finite. With p the predicted DEM and y the solver's, DEM MAE and MSE average |p_b − y_b| and (p_b − y_b)² over valid pixel-targets and the 18 bins b, in 10^26 cm^-5 and its square. The total-emission error is a ratio of sums,

$$ \text{EM error} = \frac{\sum_{\text{pixels}} \left| \sum_b p_b - \sum_b y_b \right|}{\sum_{\text{pixels}} \sum_b y_b}, $$

so bright pixels weigh most in it. W1 treats each DEM, normalised to unit total, as a distribution over logT and measures the area between the two cumulative distributions, in dex:

$$ W_1 = \sum_{b=1}^{17} \left| P_b - Y_b \right| \Delta, \qquad P_b = \frac{\sum_{j \le b} p_j}{\sum_j p_j}, \quad Y_b = \frac{\sum_{j \le b} y_j}{\sum_j y_j}, \quad \Delta = 0.1\ \text{dex}, $$

averaged over the pixels where both DEMs have a positive total. It says where the emission sits in temperature, whatever its amount. DEM MSE, EM error and W1 follow the supervised side's table script; DEM MAE comes from our diagnostic on the same pixels and mask.

4.4 AIA reconstruction

Every DEM, the label-free model's, the supervised model's and the solver's, is pushed through the 18-bin response, ŷ = R·DEM, and compared with the six observed intensities of the same pixel. AIA MAE and MSE average |ŷ_c − o_c| and (ŷ_c − o_c)² over valid pixel-targets and channels, in DN/s and (DN/s)², on one mask per track: a finite solver DEM, six finite observations and finite reconstructions from both models. Both are in raw DN/s, so channels count by brightness: the 171 and 193 Å cutoffs are 144 and 160 times the 94 Å cutoff. The solver's own reconstruction is not exact, since BP only has to land inside the band. By channel and band the analyses report Σŷ_c/Σo_c over the band's pixels, where 1.00 is exact; "flare-core 94 Å reproduced" is this ratio for 94 Å at flare cores, and "flare-core emission" is the predicted total emission there over the solver's.

4.5 Percentiles and the solver's own scatter

The per-pixel error is the squared error summed over the 18 bins, one value per valid pixel-target. We report its median (the median pixel error), p90, p99 and p99.9, read from a histogram of log10 SSE in 0.02-dex bins and so good to about 2% (the final BP model also has a 0.0001-dex histogram, noted under Table 5.1), together with the share of the total held by the worst 1% of pixels and by flare cores. Percentiles come first because the error is heavy-tailed. On the test split in August, one pixel in five million held 94.0% of a model's mean per-pixel BP loss (2.09 × 10^8 of 2.22 × 10^8): that model's mean, 44.32, was four times the patch CNN's 11.27, yet it was lower at every percentile. For the final BP model, flare cores hold 92.0% of the DEM squared error, so DEM MSE mostly reports them. We give both.

The five targets also set a floor that no deterministic emulator can beat. They share one input, so a model predicts the same DEM for all of them. Where several targets cover the same block (64% of blocks are covered by two to five), the model's MSE over those targets splits exactly into the squared distance to the mean solver DEM and the variance of the solver's DEMs across targets, the solver's own scatter. For the final BP model the scatter is 2.0% of the model's MSE on those pixels, 1.4% on Bright pixels, 43.9% on Quiet and 0.3% at flare cores; for the ElasticNet model it is 19.1%, 8.2%, 48.6% and 0.09%. The Bright and flare-core error is the model's, not label noise, while about half of the Quiet error is the solver disagreeing with itself. With 2.3 targets per pixel on average the variance is underestimated, so these shares are lower bounds.

5. Results

Every number in this section is measured on the shared test set of section 4: 153 images (86 distinct days) never used for training, with five solver targets per block, 705 million valid pixel-targets on the BP track and 802 million on the ElasticNet track. "Label-free" means the final BP model (width 680, 1.5M parameters, square root plus 12 Fourier frequencies, the stiff band, 120 epochs, clamp pixels kept in training with their clamped channels freed from the band) and the ElasticNet model (width 336, 409k parameters, same input, 40 epochs, clamp pixels excluded). "The 409k stiff-band model" is the earlier BP model (width 336, same input and band, 120 epochs then 120 more continued from that checkpoint, clamp pixels excluded); it is kept as a comparison, and sections 7 and 8, where it is the model under analysis, call it "the adopted BP model". "Supervised" is the supervised side's emulator for the same solver, scored on the same pixels against the same solver DEMs. DEM MSE is the squared error per temperature bin averaged over pixels, in units of (10^26 cm^-5)^2; the per-pixel error behind the percentiles is the squared error summed over the 18 bins. Lower is better everywhere except the two flare-core rows, where closer to 100% is better. The tables carry the final model's numbers; the figures of this section and section 6 were drawn for the 409k stiff-band model, as their captions say.

On BP, the final model wins four of the six headline measures (DEM MAE, EM error, W1 and AIA MSE); the supervised model keeps DEM MSE and AIA MAE. It also wins the median, p90, p99, flare-core emission and flare-core 94 Å, and is level on Quiet MSE. The supervised model's lead on DEM MSE is a factor of 1.2 and comes entirely from flare cores (section 5.2). One pixel holds 6.0% of the final model's DEM MSE, which is 1.02 without it; we have not computed the same removal for the supervised model. The lead on AIA MAE should be read with the solver in view: the BP solver's own AIA MAE on the same pixels is 4.26 DN/s (MSE 61.9), higher than either network's, because BP only has to land inside the band, so AIA MAE on this track measures something the solver itself does not optimise.

Against the 409k stiff-band model, the final model lowers DEM MSE from 1.75 to 1.08 and the median pixel error from 0.036 to 0.031, and raises flare-core emission from 93% to 96.7% and flare-core 94 Å from 77% to 88%. It pays for that on the AIA fit (AIA MSE 148 against 103, AIA MAE 3.54 against 3.48) and slightly on W1 (0.070 against 0.068), p99 (25.7 against 24.5) and Quiet MSE (0.033 against 0.032). Against the old model it improves every measure except the median pixel error (0.031 against 0.026) and AIA MSE (148 against 83).

On ElasticNet, the label-free model is ahead on all twelve measures. The narrowest is DEM MSE (0.310 against 0.318); the widest is AIA MAE (0.56 against 6.32, eleven times lower). The ElasticNet solver's own AIA MAE is 1.41 DN/s, so here the label-free model reproduces the observations more closely than the solver it emulates.

On the typical BP pixel the final model is 3.6 times closer to the solver than the supervised model (median 0.031 against 0.112). It stays ahead up to the 99th percentile (p90 1.82 against 1.95, p99 25.7 against 26.9). The order flips only in the last 0.1% (p99.9 169 against 162), and because the error is so heavy-tailed those pixels set the mean: the worst 1% of pixels hold 96.4% of the final model's BP squared error and 95.2% of the supervised model's, and flare cores alone, one pixel in 10,000, hold 92.0% and 90.0%. Without flare cores the final model is ahead, 0.087 against 0.091 (the 409k stiff-band model was behind, 0.102). On ElasticNet the label-free model is ahead at every percentile, and flare cores hold 44.5% of its error against 33.9% of the supervised model's; without them it leads by a wider margin (0.172 against 0.210).

What remains at BP flare cores is a shortfall in height rather than a misplaced curve: the final model holds 96.7% of the solver's emission there, its peak height is 0.89 of the solver's (supervised 0.91), its mean logT shift is -0.01 dex, and 83% of its squared error there lies along the solver's curve. The 409k stiff-band model held 92.6% and 66%; the old model held 40% and 23%, and shifted 0.18 dex cooler. The final model flags fewer flare-core pixels as multi-peaked than the solver (14.2% against 18.3%; the supervised model 12.8%; the 409k stiff-band model drew too many, 25.4%). Section 8 takes up the multi-peaked DEMs.

Each DEM is pushed back through the response matrix and compared with the six observed channels. Pooled over all valid pixels, the BP track gives AIA MAE / MSE of 3.54 / 148 for the final model, 2.95 / 157 for the supervised model and 4.26 / 61.9 for the solver; the ElasticNet track gives 0.56 / 161, 6.32 / 598 and 1.41 / 134. At flare cores the per-channel picture is the following.

On BP the final model reproduces 131, 171, 193 and 211 Å at flare cores to within 1% and over-reproduces 335 Å by 4%, as the solver does. The one gap is 94 Å, the channel that sees the hot plasma: 88% of the observed signal against the solver's 92% and the supervised model's 85% (409k stiff-band model 77%, old model 23%). The supervised model is now further from the observation on every channel but 335 Å (0.96), and 22% short on 171 Å. Away from flare cores the final model tracks the solver band by band, including the solver's own shortfall on the faint channels where the band permits it (94 Å at 0.3 to 1 times the cutoff: 0.81 label-free, 0.82 solver; 131 Å below 0.03 times the cutoff: 0.29 and 0.32), whereas the supervised model does not follow the solver there (131 Å at 1.65 on the faintest band).

On ElasticNet the solver itself reproduces only 55% of 94 Å at flare cores, and the label-free model reproduces the channels the way its solver does, within 3 points on every channel (94 Å 53% against 55%). The supervised model falls 24% to 32% short on five channels and reaches 48% on 94 Å. On the 409k stiff-band model the BP 94 Å gap was a training gap and not a loss gap: section 6 shows the best answer under the stiff loss reproduces 93% of 94 Å at the validation flare cores. The same check has not been run on the final model.

Spatial context does not help: the earlier evidence. On the four-day, 128 by 128 crop data the patch CNN looked better than a capacity-matched centre-pixel MLP in sample (sparsity score 1.70 against 1.89, solver 1.79), but that edge came from scoring pixels of days it had trained on. Leave-one-day-out, training on three days and scoring the fourth, gave held-out sparsity scores of 1.59, 1.78, 1.83 and 1.96 for the MLP against 1.64, 1.61, 1.83 and 2.31 for the CNN: the MLP wins two folds (including the X1.6 flare day), ties one and loses one (quiet sun), with the better held-out MAE on three of four. Re-scoring both on 400 held-out pixels per day gave DEM MAE 0.042 for the MLP against 0.047 for the CNN (W1 0.043 against 0.048 dex). The scaled comparison above is the fifth look at the question, and none has found a CNN advantage on unseen images, so the final models take one pixel and no neighbourhood.

6. Flare cores: the failure and the fix

Flare cores, the pixels at 32 times the Bright cutoff and above, are about one pixel in 10,000 of the shared test set (69,283 of 705 million BP pixel-targets) and hold most of the BP DEM squared error for every model (section 5.2). On the BP track the old model failed there, and the cause was the loss, not training: under the original band weight (μ = 1) the best answer under the loss leaves the hot flare plasma out of the DEM, and the old model had already reached it. A stiffer band (μ = 100), chosen on validation, makes the loss ask for the hot plasma, and longer training takes the network most of the way there; the final BP model, wider and with clamp pixels in training, goes further (section 6.7). This section follows the work in order, so it is mostly about the 409k stiff-band model that came first. The ElasticNet track never had this failure (Appendix B).

6.1 The failure

At flare cores the old model (width 336, log1p input, μ = 1, 40 epochs) held 40% of the solver's emission. Its peaks were 23% as high as the solver's, its mean logT 0.18 dex cooler, its curves almost twice as wide (an emission-weighted width of 0.41 dex against 0.23), and 83% of them had extra peaks, against 18% of the solver's. Flare cores held 90.5% of its DEM squared error, but the supervised model puts 90.0% of its error there too: that concentration is what squared error does to DEMs a thousand times larger than typical. The label-free defect was the amount, with 97.6% of the flare-core error lying along the solver's curve rather than across it.

The AIA reconstruction showed which plasma was missing. At flare cores the old model's DEM reproduced 171, 193 and 211 Å to within 2%, as the solver's did, but only 23% of the observed 94 Å, 76% of 131 Å and 67% of 335 Å, where the solver reproduced 92%, 101% and 104%. 94 Å is the channel that sees hot flare plasma (logT about 6.9, 8 MK): where the solver draws a tall peak at logT 6.8 to 6.9, the old model draws a low bump near 6.3 to 6.4 and a tail near 7.0.

Two other explanations were ruled out: the solver's own scatter across re-solves of a block is 0.38% of the old model's Bright error (0.09% at flare cores), and pixels where the solver's DEM has two or more peaks and the model's one hold 1.25% of its squared error, so neither label noise nor missed second peaks is the cause. The diagnosis was first made in September on an earlier width-232 model trained on the fixed pixel sample of Appendix C (41% of the emission, 24% of 94 Å).

Because the network fit the cool channels and missed 94 Å, it seemed to be failing its own objective, which asks for every channel inside its band: a training problem. Hence the three suggestions: show it more flare cores, train it longer, make it bigger.

6.2 Training-side suggestions that did not help

Each suggestion was one change to a common recipe: width 336, fresh pixels, 40 epochs, μ = 1, and the square root plus 12 Fourier frequencies input the follow-up adopted for both tracks. This base is slightly worse than the old model (DEM MSE 4.56 against 4.28, flare-core emission 35% against 40%). Oversampling draws pixels in proportion to brightness (clipped to 1 to 1,000 times the Bright cutoff), so flare cores rise from about 1 in 8,900 training pixels to 1 in 1,060, about 8.4 times as often. The 10M model is 1,800 wide (10.1M parameters).

Table 6.1. The suggestions on the original loss (μ = 1), shared test set.

BP run, μ = 1 DEM MSE DEM MAE Median pixel error AIA MSE Quiet MSE Flare-core emission Flare-core 94 Å
Base (square root + Fourier, 40 epochs) 4.56 0.106 0.023 83 0.057 35% 15%
Oversample flare cores 5.05 0.106 0.025 87 0.058 24% 9%
120 epochs 4.21 0.105 0.022 108 0.057 37% 16%
10M parameters 5.10 0.106 0.022 125 0.058 20% 8%

Away from flare cores the four runs score alike (DEM MAE 0.105 to 0.106, Quiet MSE 0.057 to 0.058). At flare cores none helps: oversampling empties the DEMs further (11% of the solver's emission on the validation flare cores, against the base's 34%), 120 epochs trims DEM MSE by 8% but moves flare-core emission only from 35% to 37% while AIA MSE rises from 83 to 108, and the 10M model holds 20%. Training harder did not move the failure, so the loss itself needed checking.

6.3 The objective gap

The BP loss is convex in the 54 weights, so each pixel has one lowest value, which an optimiser can find with no network. That minimiser is the best answer under the loss: no network can do better on that pixel. experiments/objective_gap.py finds it with L-BFGS-B (started from the network's output and from the solver's DEM, keeping the lower) on 11,954 validation pixels across the brightness bands, 6,000 of them flare cores. It then scores four answers under the same loss: the network's output, the best answer, the solver's DEM and the supervised model's DEM, the last two rewritten as the sparsest set of 54 weights that reproduces them.

Table 6.2. Flare cores of the validation split, every answer scored under the original loss (μ = 1): the sparsity term plus the band penalty.

Answer Loss Sparsity + band penalty 94 Å reproduced Emission vs solver DEM MSE
Old network 565 294 + 270 28% 38% 233,000
Best answer under the loss 463 220 + 243 26% 30% 233,000
Solver's DEM 1,125 1,119 + 6 94% 100% 0
Supervised model's DEM 1,878 1,107 + 771 91% 95% 38,000

The network had converged on its loss. Its median loss sits 0.8% to 3.6% above the best answer in every band from 0.03 to 32 times the Bright cutoff, 7.4% in the faintest band and 8.0% at flare cores, where its DEM error equals the best answer's (233,000 for both). Over all validation pixels, weighted by band as in section 6.5, its DEM MSE is 36.9, the same as the best answer's. A perfect network would land on the best answer, which reproduces 26% of 94 Å and holds 30% of the solver's emission: on this loss no training change can fix flare cores.

The loss prefers the DEM without the hot plasma. The solver's DEM keeps every channel in its band (penalty 6) and pays 1,119 in sparsity for the hot plasma; the best answer drops most of it and pays 220 plus 243 in band penalty. The loss rates the solver's DEM 2.4 times worse than a DEM without the hot plasma (1.3 to 1.5 times in the other Bright bands), so every training step at a flare core moves away from the solver. The supervised model shows it from the other side: under our loss its DEM scores worst (1,878), yet it is the closest network to the solver (DEM MSE 38,000 against 233,000). A low loss does not mean close to the solver.

Two caveats. L-BFGS-B stopped at its iteration limit on 271 of the 11,954 pixels at μ = 1; the loss is convex, so the true minimum there is at or below the value found, which can only widen the solver's deficit. And flare cores are a larger share of the validation days than of the test days (0.015% of pixels against 0.0098%), so validation values run higher than test values: compare rows, not sections.

6.4 Why: the price of hot plasma

The solver and the loss share one goal, the DEM with the smallest total weight that reproduces the six observations, and differ in how they treat the band. For the solver the band is a rule: every channel must land inside it. For the loss it is a price: a channel may land outside whenever that saves more in sparsity than it costs in band penalty.

Table 2.2 (section 2.6) gives what each channel sees per unit of plasma, a unit being 10^26 cm^-5 of emission measure (the unit of the weights, the DEM and the sparsity term). Warm plasma (1 to 1.3 MK, logT 6.0 to 6.1) lights 171, 193 and 211 Å by several to tens of DN/s per unit; it has to be in the DEM for those channels, and its 94 Å signal comes free. At flare cores most of the 94 Å signal comes from hot plasma, which lights no channel by more than 0.4 DN/s per unit (a spike at logT 6.9, 8 MK, gives 0.266 DN/s of 94 Å, 0.40 of 131 Å and 0.34 of 193 Å), so a bright 94 Å reading needs hundreds of units, all paid in the sparsity term, and only 94 and 131 Å ask for them.

Take a typical flare core, counting 94 Å alone: it reads 164 DN/s with σ = 11.5, so its band runs from 148 to 180 (half width 16.1).

Table 6.3. The worked example at μ = 1.

Option Sparsity Band penalty Total
Hot plasma in, as a spike at logT 6.9: 164 ÷ 0.266 ≈ 616 units 616 0 616
Hot plasma in, as the 0.2 dex Gaussian centred at logT 6.8: 164 ÷ 0.67 ≈ 245 units 245 0 245
Hot plasma out: 94 Å near 0, 148 below the band 0 (148 ÷ 16.1)² = 85 85

One unit of weight on a spike at logT 6.9 gives 0.266 DN/s of 94 Å, so including the hot plasma that way costs 616. The cheapest hot shape is the 0.2 dex Gaussian centred at logT 6.8, at 0.67 DN/s per unit, and including the plasma that way costs about 245. That is within 1% of the most 94 Å any basis element gives (0.676 DN/s per unit, the bound of 1.48 weight units per DN/s in section 3.3), which comes from the warm Gaussian at logT 6.1; that element also lights 171 Å by about 170 DN/s per unit, so it cannot stand in for hot plasma. Both exceed the 85 that leaving the plasma out costs at μ = 1, so the conclusion holds either way; at μ = 100 the same miss costs 8,500 and the plasma goes back in. The real price, the linear program's dual price of the 94 Å lower edge solved pixel by pixel, agrees: at the validation flare cores its median is 1.46 weight units per DN/s, at the single-edge bound, and it exceeds the bound at 49% of them (99th percentile 8.8), where another channel's upper edge also binds and makes the plasma dearer (section 3.3).

The failure grows with brightness because brighter pixels draw more of their 94 Å from hot plasma. On validation the best answer reproduces 91% of the observed 94 Å at 1 to 1.8 times the Bright cutoff, 92% at 1.8 to 3.2, 78% at 3.2 to 10, 44% at 10 to 32 and 26% at flare cores, where the solver's DEM reproduces 100%, 101%, 95%, 88% and 94%. The band itself is sound: σ follows photon counting, growing as the square root of the signal.

The same price explains why the label-free BP model emitted about 15% less than the solver even at ordinary pixels, a September finding left unexplained. Inside the band nothing pulls a channel toward its observation, so the sparsity term drags the emission down to the band's lower edge, where the solver's answer also sits; a squared penalty has zero slope at that edge, so with a finite μ it always pays to go a little past it. At 0.3 to 1 times the Bright cutoff the best answer emits 0.855 of the solver's emission at μ = 1, then 0.886, 0.941, 0.981 and 1.002 at μ = 3, 10, 30 and 100 (the first screen, on a sample of test pixels; the validation repeat gives 0.861 at μ = 1 and 1.009 at μ = 100). The old network sat at 0.866 in that sample. Over the full test set the old model emits 0.848 of the solver's emission, the 409k stiff-band model 0.984 and the final BP model 0.988.

6.5 The μ screen on validation

The screen tests the loss, not a network. For each μ it solves every validation pixel's best answer and scores it against the solver's DEMs, asking how close to the solver a network that learned this loss perfectly would get. The DEM error is the DEM MSE with each brightness band weighted by its share of the validation split; the Quiet MSE is the same over the bands below the Bright cutoff.

Table 6.4. The μ screen: the best answer under each loss on the validation split, with the supervised model (a trained network) for reference.

Loss DEM error Quiet MSE Flare-core 94 Å Flare-core emission
μ = 1 (original) 36.9 0.076 26% 30%
μ = 10 10.8 0.037 81% 90%
μ = 30 5.10 0.032 89% 97%
μ = 100 2.32 0.041 93% 100%
μ = 300 1.80 0.048 94% 101%
Supervised model 6.10 0.054 91% 95%

Stiffer helps bright pixels and costs faint ones. The DEM error falls to a minimum near μ = 300 (1.89 at 200, 1.80 at 300, 2.16 at 1,000). The Quiet MSE is lowest at μ = 20 to 30 (0.031 to 0.032) and rises beyond: at faint pixels the band is mostly noise, and a stiff band makes the best answer chase it. At a flare core, by contrast, a price 100 times higher works like the solver's rule.

μ = 100 takes most of the gain (DEM error 2.32) with the Quiet MSE still below the supervised model's (0.041 against 0.054); μ = 300 lowers the DEM error only to 1.80 and raises the Quiet MSE to 0.048. The flare-core 94 Å column, which compares the reconstruction with the observation and so needs no solver DEM, plateaus at μ = 100 (93%, then 94% at 300 and 95% at 1,000). The stiff band is still not the solver's rule: at the validation flare cores it rates the solver's DEM about 1.3 times worse than its best answer (1,688 against 1,264), but that best answer now holds the hot plasma.

A second candidate (μ = 30 with the sparsity term divided by the square root of brightness on Bright pixels) screened nearly as well, DEM error 1.95, but trained worse (section 6.6). μ is one scalar chosen on validation with the solver's DEMs, like any loss weight; training never sees them. An earlier screen on test pixels was repeated on validation, which kept μ = 100, and the choice rests on validation alone. Section 3.3 gives the theory: the band violation at the best answer falls as 1/μ, so μ follows from the response matrix, the noise and a chosen tolerance, with no solver DEM.

6.6 The stiff-band runs

The recipe stays the same (width 336, square root plus 12 Fourier frequencies, fresh pixels, clamp pixels excluded); the runs vary the training length, the sampling and the size. The row above the supervised model in Table 6.5 repeats the 680-wide run with clamp pixels kept (section 7.1).

BP run DEM MSE Median pixel error AIA MSE Quiet MSE Flare-core emission Flare-core 94 Å Validation error
Original loss, base (reference) 4.56 0.023 83 0.057 35% 15% 39.7
40 epochs 2.37 0.062 44 0.035 89% 68% 20.1
120 epochs 2.00 0.041 44 0.032 92% 75% 17.8
240 epochs from scratch 1.74 0.036 591 0.035 91% 73% 14.0

The band alone halves the DEM MSE (4.56 to 2.37) and lifts flare-core emission from 35% to 89%. Training then becomes the limit: at the validation flare cores the 40-epoch network's loss sits a median 118% above its best answer (the old network on the old loss: 8%). Longer training therefore helps; after 120 epochs the gap is 47%, the DEM MSE 2.00 and the flare-core 94 Å 75%.

240 epochs from scratch misfits rare pixels. It keeps improving the DEM (MSE 1.74, validation error 14.0), but its AIA MSE rises from 44 to 591 and its Quiet MSE from 0.032 to 0.035: a few pixels break the band badly, and on the validation flare cores its mean band penalty is 129 times the 120-epoch model's.

120 + 120 epochs, continued, is the 409k stiff-band model, the best BP model until the clamp runs. Warm-started from the 120-epoch checkpoint with a fresh cosine schedule, it gets the same DEM gains (MSE 1.75, median pixel error 0.036) while holding the AIA MSE at 103, below the supervised model's 157, with a flare-core band penalty 13 times the 120-epoch model's. It improves on the 120-epoch model in every measure except AIA MAE and AIA MSE. Not chosen: 120 epochs alone (AIA MSE 44 but DEM MSE 2.00) and 240 from scratch.

Nothing else helps. Oversampling still hurts (DEM MSE 2.50, median pixel error 0.071). The 10M and 680-wide models blow up on rare pixels while their median pixel error stays low (section 5.4). Section 7.1 shows which pixels, and that keeping them in training takes the 680-wide model from DEM MSE 897 to 1.08: that run is the final BP model. log1p input is worse than square root plus Fourier (DEM MSE 3.23 against 2.37). Gradient clipping at norm 1 fires on every step on the stiff band (90% of steps on the original loss); without it AIA fits better (AIA MSE 36) but every DEM measure worsens (DEM MSE 3.20). The second screen candidate trained worse than μ = 100 (validation error 22.4 against 20.1). μ = 300, on the same 120-epoch recipe, trailed μ = 100 at every matched epoch (validation DEM MAE 0.114 against 0.088 at epoch 48, 0.099 against 0.079 at epoch 76) and was stopped after about 90 epochs, never scored on the test set.

With the stiff band alone the plasma is back at the right temperature: 93% of the solver's emission (supervised 92%), a mean shift of -0.01 dex, W1 down from 0.255 to 0.033 dex, and 131 Å reproduced as the solver does. Spurious extra peaks no longer carry the error: pixels where the solver's DEM has one peak and the model's several held 42.0% of the old model's squared error and hold 3.5% of this model's (supervised 1.4%), though it still draws extra peaks on 25% of flare-core curves against the solver's 18% (section 8). Figure 5.1 shows this model at the same twelve pixels as Figure 6.1.

What was left is height at the very top. The 409k stiff-band model tracks the solver's peak up to a height of about 100 (0.97 of it at 32 to 100), then falls behind: 0.81 at 100 to 320, 0.61 at 320 to 1,000, 0.51 at 1,000 to 3,200 and 0.40 above 3,200. The old model fell from 0.77 to 0.095 over the same range; the supervised model holds 0.89 to 0.93, then 0.71 above 3,200. The 269 pixel-targets above 3,200 hold 73.1% of its DEM squared error.

By brightness band (Table 5.4 in section 5.2), its DEM MSE is 0.55 of the supervised model's on the faintest pixels and 2.02 at flare cores; the old model's ratios ran from 0.64 to 17.5.

What remained on the 409k stiff-band model.

  • Flare cores held 94.2% of its DEM squared error and set the BP DEM MSE gap: 1.75 against 0.91 (a factor of 1.9), and 0.102 against 0.091 without them (section 5.2).
  • The shortfall was in 94 Å: 77% of the observed signal against the solver's 92%; 131, 171, 193 and 211 Å are within 2%, and 335 Å is at 109% (section 5.3).
  • It was a training gap, not a loss gap. Under the stiff band the best answer reproduces 93% of 94 Å at the validation flare cores and this model 77.5%, with its loss there a median 35% above the best answer. The solver's own re-solve scatter is 0.2% of its flare-core error, so this is model error, not label noise.
  • Longer training kept closing the gap, but 240 epochs from scratch began to break the band on rare pixels.
  • Open: why the median pixel error rose from 0.026 (old model) to 0.036 while the Quiet MSE fell from 0.058 to 0.032. The final model is at 0.031 and 0.033.

The final BP model at flare cores. The final model (1.5M parameters, the stiff band, 120 epochs, clamp pixels in training) closes most of what was left. At flare cores it holds 96.7% of the solver's emission (supervised 92%), reproduces 88% of 94 Å (supervised 85%, solver 92%) and 100% of 131 Å, and peaks at 0.89 of the solver's height (supervised 0.91), with a mean shift of -0.01 dex, W1 of 0.018 dex (supervised 0.015) and extra peaks on 14% of curves (supervised 13%, solver 18%). It follows the solver's peak much further: 0.98 at 32 to 100, 0.97 at 100 to 320, 0.92 at 320 to 1,000, 0.78 at 1,000 to 3,200 and 0.53 above 3,200. Flare cores still hold 92.0% of its DEM squared error, 83.0% of the total in those same 269 pixel-targets above 3,200, and its DEM MSE there is 1.22 times the supervised model's. That is the whole of the remaining BP gap: 1.08 against 0.91 overall, and 0.087 against 0.091 without flare cores (section 5.2). Tables 5.1 and 5.5 give the rest.
