7. Failure analysis

Three questions from the last review are answered here: which pixels blow up when the network gets bigger, and why a bigger network should fail at all (7.1); what the pixels at the low end of the AIA joint distributions are (7.2); and what happens at the pixels where no DEM fits the noise band, which is where relaxing the constraint matters (7.3). The first two have the same root: a small set of inputs that training never contained.

7.1 Which pixels blow up, and why bigger networks fail there

Every model's DEM error is concentrated in a few pixels, but the larger models concentrate it far more (Table 7.1). On the shared test set the 409k stiff-band model's worst 0.01% of pixels hold 95% of its squared error; the 1.5M-parameter model trained on the same loss (680 wide, μ = 100, 120 epochs) puts 99.7% of its error in its worst 100 pixels, out of 705M.

Table 7.1. Concentration of the DEM squared error on the shared test set (sum over the 18 bins, per pixel), by model.

Track Model DEM MSE Worst 0.01% of pixels Worst 100 pixels
BP 409k, adopted 1.75 95.1% 67.3%
BP 1.5M, μ = 100, 120 epochs 897 99.99% 99.7%
BP 10M, μ = 100 35.7 99.7% 98.0%
BP 10M, μ = 1 5.10 91.5% 50.1%
ElasticNet 409k, final 0.310 44.8% 29.1%
ElasticNet 722k, log1p input 3.24 94.7% 70.0%
ElasticNet 1.4M, log1p input 36.2 99.5% 68.7%
ElasticNet 10M 2,062 99.99% 96.9%

Two kinds of worst pixel. The 409k stiff-band model's worst 1,000 distinct inputs are 993 flare cores, and the 10M BP model's worst 1,000 overlap them almost entirely (Jaccard 0.88): these are the brightest flare cores, hard for every model. The pixels that make the large models blow up are different. The 1.5M model's worst 100 share only 7% with the 409k stiff-band model's (Jaccard 0.07), and they look alike: in its worst 100 distinct inputs a median of five of the six channels read exactly zero, and in 56% only one channel has signal, always 94 Å, at a median 3.0 DN/s, 28 times the median of its eight neighbours (more than 5 times in every case). The ElasticNet 10M model's worst 100 are the same kind (64% a lone 94 Å reading of about 4.2 DN/s, 57 times its neighbours). The ElasticNet 722k and 1.4M log1p models fail on a related set: in about a quarter of their worst 100 the lone channel is 131 Å, at about 200 DN/s, 1,500 to 2,000 times its neighbours. Figure 7.2 shows one such pixel.

Why training never saw them. A channel that reads exactly zero is the positivity clamp of the PSF deconvolution: the deconvolved value came out negative and was set to zero. The training mask required every channel above 10⁻³ DN/s, which drops every pixel with a clamped channel. That is 40% of the valid test pixels, nearly all faint (96% of the faintest band, 2.2% at 1 to 1.8 times the Bright cutoff, none above 3.2 times), so it barely touches the pixels the metrics weigh. But it removes every input in which a channel is zero, and the lone-spike pixels are exactly such inputs. The validation loss uses the same mask, so it could not see them either (section 3.5 also notes that it covers only the first four validation images). This is why validation preferred every model larger than 409k while each of them blew up on test.

How far they are from the training data. We drew 2 million valid training pixels and measured, for each test pixel, the distance to the nearest one in standardised log intensity (Figure 7.1). Ordinary test pixels sit at a median 0.09 to 0.21 from a training pixel, depending on brightness. The 1.5M BP model's worst inputs sit at about 4.9, and the ElasticNet 10M model's at 3 to 5: twenty to fifty times further out than anything the network was fitted on. The 409k stiff-band model's worst pixels, the brightest flare cores, sit at a median 0.40 against 0.21 for flare cores in general; 19% are outside the range of the training sample in some channel. They are at the edge of the training data, not off it.

The mechanism. A per-pixel network is an interpolator. Where training pixels are dense its output is pinned by the loss; far from them nothing constrains it. A larger network has more freedom to bend between and beyond the data, and the Fourier encoding, whose purpose is to let the network represent sharp functions of its input, gives it the means. At the lone-spike inputs the larger models return DEMs up to 10⁵ times the solver's: the ElasticNet 10M model's worst 1,000 inputs have a median emission 1.6 × 10⁵ times the solver's, and the 1.5M BP model reconstructs 171 Å at more than 2 × 10⁵ times the observation at a tenth of its worst 1,000. Bigger is therefore not worse at fitting the data: the larger models match or beat 409k at the median (section 5.4). It is worse at extrapolating, and the evaluation contains inputs that training excluded.

Confirmation runs. If this is the cause, training on those inputs should remove the blow-ups. Four runs repeat existing ones with one change, the clamp pixels kept and only their clamped channels freed from the band (--clamp_mode mask).

Table 7.2. The same recipe with and without clamp pixels in training, shared test set.

Run DEM MSE, excluded DEM MSE, clamp pixels kept Note
BP 1.5M, μ = 100, 120 epochs 897 1.08 flare-core 94 Å 88%, emission 96.7%
ElasticNet 10M, 40 epochs 2,062 1.82 AIA MSE still 1.5 × 10⁵
BP 409k, μ = 100, 40 epochs 2.37 2.79 flare-core emission 85% against 89%
ElasticNet 409k, 40 epochs 0.310 0.439 AIA MSE 162 against 161

The score blow-ups are gone: two models that failed by orders of magnitude now score normally, and the 1.5M BP model is the best BP model we have, which is why it became the final model. Clamp pixels do not help the 409k models. They take a large share of each epoch's draws, and a small network pays for that: BP loses flare-core emission, and ElasticNet loses on faint pixels too (Quiet MSE 0.122 to 0.212, median pixel error 0.85 to 1.55). The ElasticNet 10M model still trails the 409k model and keeps a few wild reconstructions, so its failure is reduced rather than removed.

What the runs did not fix. The score blow-ups and the wildest reconstructions are not the same thing. On the eight full disks of the viewer, counting a pixel as wild when some channel is reconstructed above 10³ DN/s and more than 100 times its observation, the old 409k BP model has 126 wild pixels of 33.5M and the new model 124; the new model's largest overshoot is about 20 times higher (2.5 × 10⁸ against 1.2 × 10⁷). Nearly all have no solver DEM (123 of 124), because they are unsolved even at the 5 times band; training excludes unsolved pixels in either mode, so clamp masking cannot reach them, and they are absent from every DEM score. They are single-channel readings among zeros (335 Å at 1,320 DN/s, typical value about 10, with the other channels zero): not plasma. One does have a solver DEM: a lone 335 Å reading of 44 DN/s on 9 December, which alone holds 97.7% of the new model's error on that disk.

A self-check closes this. Simple input rules do not work: a clamp-plus-neighbour-spike rule flags up to 14% of all pixels, and a dominant-channel rule catches at most 79% of the wild ones. The direct test does: a DEM must reproduce what was observed, so a pixel whose reconstruction overshoots its observation by more than 100 times is flagged. This needs neither a solver nor a label, flags 124 of 33.5M pixels, and removes the outliers from the viewer's images. The scores in this report do not apply it. They would barely move: on the shared test set the wild pixels have no BP target, and the single pixel that holds 6% of the final model's DEM error (1.08, or 1.02 without it) is a real flare core, not a spike.

7.2 The low end of the AIA joint distributions

In the viewer's joint distributions of observed against reconstructed AIA, some pixels observed near 1 DN/s are reconstructed far above the diagonal by the label-free model but not by the supervised one. We counted them over the whole shared test set: observed below 1 DN/s and reconstructed above 10 times the observation (both floored at 0.5 DN/s, as in the plots).

Table 7.3. Pixels in the low cluster on the shared test set, BP track, by channel and by whose DEM puts them there. Out of 705M valid pixels.

Channel Label-free Supervised Solver Label-free cluster with that channel clamped
94 Å 0 1 0
131 Å 18,625 3,792 152,767 84%
171 Å 51 369 0 96%
193 Å 8,073 460 123,154 89%
211 Å 95 36 0 93%
335 Å 23,370 63 102,110 81%

The cluster is small: about 50,000 pixels, 0.007% of the test set. Almost all of it is the deconvolution clamp: 81% to 96% of the pixels have that very channel at exactly zero, and 96% to 100% are isolated dips against their eight neighbours. It splits into two groups.

  • 131, 193 and 335 Å: the observation is wrong, not the DEM. Here the solver's own DEM sits above the zeroed observation more often than ours (152,767 pixels against 18,625 in 131 Å) and by as much (mean 1.25 against 1.09 dex above). No DEM that fits the other five channels can produce zero in the sixth. The supervised model sits closer to the zero, because it learned these pixels from the solver's labels.
  • 171 and 211 Å: the network extrapolates. Here only our model is far off (3.4 and 1.9 dex above the observation; the solver 0.04 and 0.0; the supervised model 0.6 and 0.0). These are the lone-spike inputs of 7.1: half of the 171 Å cluster is a lone 94 Å reading of about 3.5 DN/s, 38 times its neighbours, with the five other channels zero (Figure 7.2). The solver cannot fit that 94 Å reading without lighting the zeroed channels, so it reproduces almost nothing; our network has never seen such an input and returns a large DEM.

Cosmic rays. The advisor's suggestion fits the lone spikes: a single channel reading 30 to 2,000 times its neighbours, in a patch where everything else is clamped to zero, is the signature of a residual cosmic-ray hit or a hot pixel (one image cannot tell them apart). The broader cluster is the clamp, not cosmic rays. The opposite corner, observed above 20 DN/s and reconstructed below a tenth of it, is rare for our model (25 pixels in 131 Å, 137 in 335 Å); 60% to 83% of those are isolated spikes too.

Where the clamp falls. Replaying the block positions of our test split: on the disk 26% of pixels have a clamped channel, but only in the faint channels (94 Å 12%, 335 Å 12%, 131 Å 5%, the bright three at most 0.06%); within 100 pixels of the limb 16%; off the limb 63%, in every channel.

Effect on the headline numbers. Removing the 49,991 pixels of the label-free low cluster from both models' scores changes our BP DEM MSE from 1.751 to 1.745 but our AIA MSE from 103 to 69; the supervised model's stays at 157. A model-independent mask, every pixel with a clamped channel removed (40% of pixels, nearly all faint), gives AIA MSE 108 against 256 and DEM MSE 2.88 against 1.49, higher for both because the remaining pixels are brighter on average. On ElasticNet the cluster is larger but shared with the solver (335 Å: ours 578,931, the solver's 611,921), and removing it moves AIA MSE only from 161 to 158 (supervised 598 to 593).

With clamp pixels in training. The 1.5M model's low cluster is larger, not smaller: 3.6M pixels in 171 Å, 2.0M in 193 Å and 1.1M in 211 Å, all with that channel clamped, about 5.5M pixels or 0.8% of the test set. This is what freeing a channel means: nothing pulls the reconstruction down to a zero we no longer trust, so the DEM fits the other five channels and predicts roughly 15 times the floored value in the clamped one. The JPDFs therefore show a fuller column at the floor, while the scores barely move (AIA MSE 148 with the cluster, 149 without). The high corner is nearly empty (102 pixels, all in 335 Å).

7.3 Where no DEM fits the band: relaxing the constraint

At some pixels no non-negative DEM fits all six channels within 1.4σ. The solver then widens its band to 3 times and, failing that, 5 times (fullBP.py:515), and records the level. On our clean labels the band is relaxed at 8.5% of test-split pixels (3 times) and 0.08% (5 times); 0.01% stay unsolved. On the validation sample of the μ screen we solved the linear program ourselves: every tolLevel-1 pixel is feasible at 1.4σ, and every relaxed pixel is infeasible (936 of 1,055) or numerically unsolvable (119), so the flag records infeasibility. (The solver's stored DEMs sit inside their bands to within 0.01 half-widths, a median 5 × 10⁻⁴: float rounding.)

These pixels carry the stiff band's cost. Our loss keeps the 1.4σ band everywhere. At feasible pixels the best answer under the loss moves toward the solver at every μ, in every brightness band, all the way to μ = 1,000 (at flare cores its DEM error falls from 1.8 × 10⁵ at μ = 1 to 9.5 × 10³ at 100 and 1.9 × 10³ at 1,000). At relaxed pixels it moves away, because a stiffer band forces an inconsistent observation that the solver itself gave up on (at 0.3 to 1 times Bright, 0.055 at μ = 1, 0.92 at 100, 1.29 at 1,000). The relaxed pixels are 0.5% to 12% of each band above 0.3 times Bright, but hold 70% to 90% of the best answer's DEM error at μ = 100 between 0.3 and 10 times Bright, and 46% (10 to 32 times) and 38% (flare cores) above. The U-shape of the μ screen's Quiet error (section 6.5) is entirely theirs.

Relaxing the band as the solver does. We re-solved the best answer at the relaxed pixels with the solver's own band, keeping the excess measured in units of the unrelaxed 1.4σ (experiments/relaxed_band_screen.py). The trade-off disappears (Figure 7.3, Table 7.4): every column improves monotonically with μ.

Table 7.4. The μ screen on validation with the fixed 1.4σ band and with the solver's band (excess in noise units). Population-weighted as in section 6.5.

μ DEM error, fixed DEM error, solver's band Quiet MSE, fixed Quiet MSE, solver's band Flare-core 94 Å, solver's band
10 10.9 12.1 0.037 0.027 80%
30 4.94 5.47 0.034 0.015 89%
100 2.30 2.79 0.046 0.0079 92%
300 1.78 1.11 0.053 0.0036 93%
1,000 2.17 0.63 0.055 0.0018 94%

The solver reproduces 94% of flare-core 94 Å; the supervised model's numbers on this screen are a DEM error of 6.10 and a Quiet MSE of 0.054. How the excess is measured matters: dividing it by the widened half-width instead softens the penalty 9 or 25 times in DN/s at relaxed pixels and gives flare cores back their deficit (88% of 94 Å at μ = 100).

What this means for μ. With the solver's own rule in the loss, μ has no interior optimum. The loss is the exterior penalty of the solver's program, relaxation included, and μ only sets how far outside the band the answer may sit, λ_c tσ_c/(2μ) (section 3.3). Larger is better for the best answer; the reasons to stop at a finite μ are training stiffness and the 1/μ law's diminishing returns. On the fixed band, μ = 300 trained behind μ = 100 at matched epochs (section 6.6), and the relaxed pixels, whose penalty never reaches zero, are a likely cause.

What the headline numbers see. The shared test set's BP targets are missing at 7.7% of clean-solve pixels and 12% to 13% of the noisy re-solves. The supervised side's generation command passes --zerochill, which skips the relaxation (we have the ElasticNet command; the BP rate at clean solves, 7.7%, matches our relaxed share of 8.5%), so the pixels where the band is infeasible have no BP answer and are not scored. The headline BP numbers therefore come from feasible pixels only, where the fixed and relaxed bands coincide.

The training run. We trained μ = 300 with the solver's band for 120 epochs (409k, no clamp pixels). At the relaxed pixels it does what the screen predicts: validation DEM MAE there is 0.15 against 0.50 for μ = 300 on the fixed band and 0.45 for μ = 100. It also trains faster than μ = 300 on the fixed band (0.090 against 0.099 at feasible pixels at epoch 76), but stays behind μ = 100 (0.079). On the shared test set it reaches DEM MSE 1.54, flare-core emission 96.8% and 94 Å 87%, better than the 409k μ = 100 model at 120 epochs (2.00, 92%, 75%), but Quiet MSE rises to 0.050 against 0.032, and one validation pass spiked to 4 × 10¹⁶ at epoch 40. So the relaxed band works as theory says at the pixels it targets, but a stiffer loss still costs training time on the faint majority. μ = 100 stays. A 1.5M model on the relaxed band is untested.

7.4 Summary

  • The large models' score blow-ups came from inputs training never saw: a lone channel spike, consistent with a cosmic-ray hit or hot pixel, among channels the deconvolution clamped to zero. Keeping clamp pixels in training removes them (BP 1.5M: 897 to 1.08), and that model is now the BP final. The most extreme single pixels remain, nearly all without a solver answer, and a self-check on the reconstruction flags them.
  • The rest of the low JPDF cluster (131, 193, 335 Å) is the clamp itself, where the observation is wrong and the solver's DEM disagrees with it as much as ours does.
  • The stiff band's cost on faint pixels comes from the 9% of pixels where the band is infeasible. For the best answer, relaxing the band there as the solver does removes it and μ becomes a convergence parameter. In training, the relaxed band fixes those pixels but μ = 300 still costs the faint majority, so μ = 100 stays.

8. What the network learned

The advisor asked what the final layer looks like, sorted by eigenvector. The output layer maps the last 336 hidden units to the 54 basis weights, so it can be read three ways: the weight matrix itself, the 54 outputs it produces over many pixels, and the DEMs those outputs make. We analysed all three for the adopted BP model, the ElasticNet model and, for contrast, the old BP model (μ = 1, log1p input, 40 epochs), on 611,947 validation pixels: up to 100,000 per brightness band and every flare core of the split (experiments/final_layer.py).

8.1 The output layer is low-rank, and the stiff band widened it

Table 8.1. Effective dimension of the output layer and of what it produces. The participation ratio of a spectrum is (Σλ)²/Σλ²; "for 90%" is the number of components that hold 90% of it.

BP adopted ElasticNet BP old (μ = 1)
Weight matrix (54 × 336): participation ratio of the singular values 9.5 7.4 2.9
Weight matrix: components for 90% / 99% of the energy 22 / 40 19 / 40 11 / 24
The 54 outputs over pixels: participation ratio of their correlation 13.5 6.7 5.7
Last hidden layer (336 units): components for 90% / 99% of the variance 14 / 90 11 / 57 6 / 34
DEM shapes (unit sum): components for 90% / 99% 8 / 12 10 / 15 4 / 8
The solver's DEM shapes on the same pixels 6 / 13 6 / 13

The old model's output layer was close to rank three, and its DEMs lived in a family of four shapes where the solver's need six. The stiff band tripled the layer's effective rank, and the adopted model's DEMs span as many shape directions as the solver's (8 against 6 for 90%, 12 against 13 for 99%). The 336 hidden units are far from saturated: 14 directions carry 90% of their variance. Width is not what limits the typical pixel, which agrees with section 7.1: extra width buys freedom away from the data, not accuracy on it.

8.2 Sorted by eigenvector: a hot-plasma mode

Sorting the 54 outputs by the leading eigenvector of their correlation (Figure 8.1, centre) does not produce a smooth sweep in temperature. It produces one tight block: the spikes and 0.1 dex Gaussians at logT 6.6 to 7.2, joined by the coolest spikes at logT 5.6 and 5.7, whose ten members move together with a mean correlation of 0.86. The leading direction is how much hot plasma the pixel has. The same block leads at every brightness from 0.03 to 32 times the Bright cutoff. At flare cores the leading direction shifts to the hottest elements (logT 7.0 to 7.2) together with cool 0.2 dex Gaussians, the variation that remains once hot plasma is always present. The second eigenvector separates the hottest end (7.0 to 7.2) from the cool end (5.5 to 6.2). The weight matrix's own singular vectors give the same picture: its first left singular vector orders the outputs from the spike and 0.1 dex Gaussian at logT 7.0 downward through the hot elements.

8.3 How the network uses the basis

Table 8.2. Weight by basis shape, and active elements per pixel (above 1% of the pixel's largest weight), on 20,000 validation pixels stratified by brightness. The solver's DEMs are decomposed into their fewest-weights representation.

Spike 0.1 dex Gaussian 0.2 dex Gaussian Active elements per pixel, mean (median)
BP adopted 18% 21% 61% 6.6 (6)
Solver 22% 30% 49% 5.7 (6)
BP old (μ = 1), all pixels 2% 6% 93% 4.2 (4)

The adopted model is a little less sparse than the solver: it leans on the wide Gaussians (61% of its weight against 49%) and uses about one more element per pixel. The old model built nearly every DEM from a few wide Gaussians: 93% of its weight sat on the 0.2 dex shape, at logT 6.3 to 6.4 and at 7.0, with nothing between 6.6 and 6.9, which is where the solver puts its hot plasma (section 6).

The weights also show that the 54-weight representation is not unique. The adopted model puts 25% of its weight on elements centred at logT 6.8 and 36% at 7.0, and essentially none at 6.9; the solver puts 15%, 36% and 15% there (Figure 8.1, right). Both describe the same hot bump around logT 6.9: two Gaussians either side of a bin add up to a curve centred on it. The loss scores only the light a DEM makes and its total weight, so the network is free to pick either decomposition, and the DEM error compares curves, not weights.

The ElasticNet model spreads its weight over all three shapes (27%, 36% and 36%) and about 20 elements per pixel, as the L2 term asks; its weight matrix and outputs are lower-rank than the adopted BP model's (Table 8.1).

8.4 The final 1.5M model

The sections above analyse the 409k stiff-band model. The same analysis on the final 1.5M model (width 680, clamp pixels in training) shows the same structure at slightly higher rank, with one change in the eigenvectors.

Table 8.3. The final model against the 409k stiff-band model.

Final 1.5M 409k stiff-band Solver
Weight matrix: participation ratio 10.9 9.5
Weight matrix: components for 90% / 99% 24 / 43 22 / 40
Outputs: correlation participation ratio 8.3 13.5
Last hidden layer: components for 90% / 99% 18 / 137 of 680 14 / 90 of 336
DEM shapes: components for 90% / 99% 8 / 13 8 / 12 6 / 13
Weight by shape (spike, 0.1 dex, 0.2 dex), solver's pixels 26%, 35%, 39% 18%, 21%, 61% 22%, 30%, 49%
Active elements per pixel, all pixels, mean 7.1 7.0 5.7

Doubling the width barely changes the effective dimension of the last hidden layer (18 against 14 directions for 90% of its variance), so the extra width is not spent on more directions of the typical pixel. The final model's weight shares are closer to the solver's on either side, where the 409k model leaned on the widest Gaussian, and it no longer leaves the elements at logT 6.9 empty: its weight there is 17%, between 12% at 6.8 and 13% at 7.0. Its leading eigenvector differs: the cool elements (logT 5.6 to 6.1) lead, with the hot spikes behind them, rather than one hot block. We read this as an effect of the clamp pixels, which give the network a large faint population to represent, but we have not tested that.

9. Limitations and open items

Validation. The validation loss that chose widths, inputs and checkpoints covers only the first four validation images (256 blocks, 131,072 pixels). With clamp pixels excluded it never contains a pixel with a clamped channel, and it preferred every model larger than 409k, each of which blew up on test (sections 3.5 and 7.1). The clamp-mask runs keep clamp pixels in that sample, but it is still those four images, and their losses are not comparable with the earlier ones. So three choices rest on test evidence: the ElasticNet width, the ElasticNet epochs and the final BP model itself. No 409k clamp run at 120 epochs exists to compare it with. Validating on every pixel of the validation split, clamp pixels included, is the fix.

Clamp pixels. Pixels with a clamped channel are 40% of valid pixels, nearly all faint. The final BP model trains on them with the clamped channels freed from the band; the ElasticNet model excludes them, because at 409k they cost more than they give (DEM MSE 0.310 to 0.439, Quiet MSE 0.122 to 0.212). Only the 10M ElasticNet model has been trained with them at a larger size: its DEM MSE falls from 2,062 to 1.82, still behind the 409k model, with AIA MSE 1.5 × 10⁵. An ElasticNet 1.5M model with clamp pixels is untested. A freed channel is not fitted, so the final BP model predicts about 15 times the floored value there: the low cluster of its AIA joint distributions holds about 5.5M pixels, 0.8% of the test set, and barely moves the scores (section 7.2).

Remaining outliers and the self-check. Keeping clamp pixels removes the score blow-ups, not the most extreme single pixels. On the eight full disks of the viewer the final BP model has 124 wild pixels of 33.5M, about the same as the 409k stiff-band model's 126, and its largest overshoot is about 20 times higher. Of the 124, 123 have no solver DEM: they are unsolved even at the 5 times band, so no training mask reaches them and no DEM score sees them. The one that has a solver DEM alone holds 97.7% of the final model's error on its disk (section 7.1). Simple input rules do not isolate these pixels. A self-check does, with no solver and no label: flag a pixel whose reconstruction overshoots its observation by more than 100 times. The viewer applies it; the scores in this report do not. It flags pixels without repairing them, so a user still needs to treat those pixels as missing.

The band's rule. Our loss keeps the 1.4σ band where the solver relaxed it (8.5% of our test split). Section 7.3 shows that the solver's own rule, with the excess measured in noise units, removes the trade-off for the best answer, so μ has no interior optimum there. The one training run on it (409k, μ = 300, 120 epochs) confirms this at the relaxed pixels (validation DEM MAE 0.15 against 0.50 on the fixed band) and improves flare cores, but Quiet MSE rises to 0.050 against 0.032, and one validation pass spiked to 4 × 10¹⁶, so μ = 100 stays. A 1.5M model on the relaxed band is untested. The per-pixel weight and the L1 exact penalty of section 3.3 are untested in training.

The evaluation protocol. The shared test set's BP targets exclude the pixels where the band is infeasible (7.7% of clean solves, 12% to 13% of re-solves), so the BP headline numbers say nothing about them. The four re-solves add Gaussian noise of 0.5σ, not σ (the generation command uses the default --noisescale 0.5). Our network's basis truncates each Gaussian below 4% of its peak while the solver's runs keep the tails (--notrunc); the difference is at most 2.1% of an element's emission and moves the price bounds by less than 1%. The ElasticNet solver floors its residual scale at 0.5 DN/s and our loss does not; 1.4σ falls below 0.5 DN/s at under 0.1% of pixels.

Flare cores. The final BP model still holds 92% of its DEM error in flare cores, where it reproduces 88% of 94 Å against the solver's 92% and its DEM MSE is 1.22 times the supervised model's (section 6.7). On the 409k model a continuation of 120 more epochs improved flare cores; a continuation of the 1.5M model is untested. The objective-gap measurement of section 6 has not been repeated on the final model, so how much of its 94 Å gap is training has not been measured.

The analysis of the network. Section 8 analyses the 409k stiff-band model in detail and the final model in summary (section 8.4). The figures of sections 5 and 6 also show the 409k stiff-band model and have not been redrawn.

Not addressed. Inference speed against the solver is unmeasured. The uncertainty head, which needs a distribution over DEMs rather than one answer, and the AIA plus XRT models are outside this report.

10. Conclusions

We set out to replace a per-pixel DEM solver with a network that never sees its output. Five conclusions follow.

Label-free training is enough. A per-pixel MLP that reads one pixel's six AIA intensities and is trained only on the solver's objective matches or beats a supervised emulator trained on the solver's DEMs. The 409k ElasticNet model is ahead on all six headline measures. The 1.5M BP model is ahead on four of six, loses DEM MSE (1.08 against 0.91) and AIA MAE (3.54 against 2.95), and on the typical pixel is 3.6 times closer to the solver (median pixel error 0.031 against 0.112). Without flare cores its DEM MSE is below the supervised model's (0.087 against 0.091). Solver DEMs were needed only to score it, and when the ElasticNet settings changed it needed retraining, not new labels.

Check the loss before the training. BP's one failure, flare cores, was in the loss. The network sat close to its loss's per-pixel optimum, and with the band weight at μ = 1 that optimum leaves the hot plasma out, because only 94 and 131 Å ask for it, at under 0.4 DN/s per unit. No training change on that loss could fix it. A stiffer band (μ = 100, chosen on validation) did: flare-core emission rose from 40% of the solver's to 93% with the 409k stiff-band model and 96.7% with the final model, and flare-core 94 Å from 23% to 88% (the solver 92%). Penalty-method theory gives the band violation as λ_c tσ_c/(2μ), and on validation the measured violation matches it pixel by pixel (median ratio 1.00), so μ follows from the response, the noise and a chosen tolerance rather than from a search.

Relaxing the band works where it should, and μ = 100 stays. The theory does not cover the 9% of pixels where no DEM fits the band. The solver relaxes its band there, and those pixels carry the stiff band's cost on faint pixels. Doing the same in the loss turns μ, for the best answer, from a trade-off into a convergence parameter: the best answer approaches the solver monotonically as μ grows. Training confirms this at the relaxed pixels: a 409k run at μ = 300 on the relaxed band has validation DEM MAE 0.15 there against 0.50 on the fixed band. It does not pay overall: a stiffer loss still costs the faint majority (Quiet MSE 0.050 against 0.032), so μ = 100 stays. The headline BP numbers do not see this choice directly, since the shared test set has no BP answer at pixels where the band is infeasible.

Larger models blow up on scores only without the clamp pixels. At scale the per-pixel MLP beat the patch CNN at every percentile of the training loss on both tracks, so spatial context is not needed. Larger MLPs improve the typical pixel a little, and trained with clamp pixels excluded they failed by orders of magnitude on a few rare pixels. Those pixels are inputs training never contained: a lone channel reading tens to thousands of times its neighbours, consistent with a cosmic-ray hit or hot pixel, among channels the deconvolution clamped to zero. The training mask dropped 40% of pixels, not the 5% first estimated, and so did the validation loss, so neither could see them. Keeping those pixels, with only the clamped channels freed from the band, took the 1.5M BP model from DEM MSE 897 to 1.08, the best BP model we have, and the 10M ElasticNet model from 2,062 to 1.82. The small models lose from those pixels (BP 409k 2.37 to 2.79 at 40 epochs, ElasticNet 409k 0.310 to 0.439), so the ElasticNet final stays at 409k without them. The 10M ElasticNet model still trails it, and an ElasticNet 1.5M model with clamp pixels is untested.

The remaining error is concentrated, and the worst pixels can be flagged. Flare cores are one pixel in 10,000 and hold 92% of the final BP model's squared error and 90% of the supervised model's. Up to the 99th percentile the final model is ahead of the supervised one: percentiles, not means, describe the typical pixel. What is left at flare cores is height at the very top (0.53 of the solver's peak above 3,200, 0.71 for the supervised model) and 94 Å. The low end of the AIA joint distributions is the clamp: where a channel was zeroed the observation is wrong, and the solver's DEM disagrees with it as much as ours on 131, 193 and 335 Å. With the clamped channels freed that column of pixels grows (about 5.5M, 0.8% of the test set) and barely moves the scores (AIA MSE 148 with it, 149 without). The most extreme single pixels remain, 124 of 33.5M on the viewer's eight disks, nearly all without a solver DEM. A self-check needs neither a solver nor a label: a DEM must reproduce what was observed, so a pixel whose reconstruction overshoots its observation by more than 100 times is flagged.

Section 9 lists what stays open, including the unmeasured inference speed and the three choices set with test evidence: the ElasticNet width and epochs, and the final BP model.

Appendix

A. History

The June and early-July results come from four days, each a crop near disk centre (the X2.1 flare of 2011-09-06, quiet Sun on 2012-06-03, moderate activity on 2013-11-13 and the X1.6 flare of 2014-09-10). Every scaled run from 31 July to 2 October trained on one fixed sample of pixels (Appendix C).

Which loss (June). Before any network, five losses were optimised directly, pixel by pixel, on the four days. The fit-only losses (χ² plus smoothness, maximum entropy, Tikhonov) reconstruct AIA far more closely than BP (AIA MAE 0.40 to 0.44 against BP's 5.2) yet land far from its DEM (DEM MAE against BP 0.18 to 0.20), while BP's own terms, the band penalty with L1 sparsity, land on it (0.034, or 0.043 with an added fit term). Six channels underdetermine an 18-bin DEM, so the tie-breaker decides the shape, and a network meant to emulate a solver has to train on its objective.

The first network (19 June). A per-pixel MLP of width 256 (213k parameters) on the six raw intensities, trained on the band-penalty loss over about 221,000 pixels. Its curves were described at the time as noisy; retrained with the unchanged code on 2026-10-03, they are single-peaked (1.00 to 1.03 local maxima per curve, none with three or more, against BP's 1.12 to 1.19). Its real deficit was accuracy: on 400 held-out pixels per day its DEM MAE against BP is 0.078, against the patch CNN's 0.047 (W1 0.055 against 0.048 dex).

The patch CNN (27 June). A CNN on the 9 by 9 neighbourhood (about 1.5M parameters) predicting the same 54 weights, trained first on one crop (sparsity score on the 54 weights 1.30, BP 1.84), then amortised over the four days (1.47 to 1.86 on held-out pixels, BP 1.67 to 1.97), then with the neighbourhood zeroed on 10% of batches so that it also works on a single pixel. The held-out pixels came from the training days, so none of this was a test.

The ablation (2 July) and leave-one-day-out (11 July). Four variants of about 1.45M parameters on the same loss and days: the patch CNN, a centre-pixel MLP (1.43M), a flat-patch MLP and a CNN on a fixed random permutation of the patch, with sparsity scores (BP 1.79) of 1.70, 1.89, 1.95 and 1.88; the patch CNN on the ElasticNet loss scored 2.28. The centre-pixel MLP drew smooth curves and was the closest to BP (DEM MAE 0.042 against the CNN's 0.047), so the first MLP's gap was capacity or input scaling (the two were not separated), not missing neighbours. Leave-one-day-out then removed the CNN's in-sample edge (section 5.4). Its weak fold was the X1.6 flare day (peaks at logT about 6.1 against BP's 6.4), with only one other flare day in training.

The first bimodal check (11 July). On the crops 5.1% to 9.1% of the scanned BP DEMs were bimodal, and only 6 of 120 studied pixels stayed bimodal across at least 80% of 20 photon-noise perturbations, all on the flare days. The conclusion that bimodality was mostly noise did not survive the move to scale (2 August, below).

Labels at scale (31 July). BP and ElasticNet were run on 1,223 Hofmeister-deconvolved AIA images (2,446 cluster jobs, zero errors, 888 GB per solver), split in time into 917 training, 153 validation and 153 test images. Dropping BP's --zerochill flag, which disables its retry at a wider tolerance, cut the unsolved pixels from 10.2% to 0.02%: photon noise narrows the relative band as pixels brighten until the LP becomes infeasible, so the flag had discarded mostly bright pixels. About 4.4% of pixels carry a hard zero in 171 or 193 Å, the two brightest channels, which only the deconvolution's positivity clamp can produce, and BP fits a DEM to them anyway. Pixels with any channel at or below MIN_OBS = 10^-3 DN/s, three decades below the faintest channel's median (94 Å, 0.76 DN/s), were then dropped from training at an estimated cost of about 5% of pixels; the count over all six channels, made in October, is 40% (sections 3.4 and 7.1).

The collapse and its fix (31 July). The first four full-disk runs exited cleanly and predicted an identically zero DEM. The architectures had been validated on crops spanning about one decade of intensity; the full disk runs from the 10^-3 DN/s floor off the limb to about 10^4 DN/s in flare cores. Fed raw intensities, the untrained network predicted AIA about seven times above the band, the loss at step 0 was 5.3 × 10^13, and the output softplus started so far negative (pre-activation -139.8) that in float32 its gradient was exactly zero. By step 60, 98% of outputs were dead, and the runs then repeated a bit-identical epoch loss for eleven epochs. Gradient clipping cannot help, as Adam normalises the step size. The fix has four parts: log1p on the network input only, with the loss, the band and every metric left in DN/s; a linear learning-rate warm-up (500 steps, raised to 3,000 when the CNN on the ElasticNet loss still died at initialisation); a clamped softplus whose pre-activation is floored at -20, so its gradient never vanishes; and a guard that stops a run whose sparsity is zero or whose epoch loss repeats exactly. A 64-block smoke test could not have caught the failure, because it never drew a flare pixel.

First converged scaled runs (31 July). With the fix all four runs converged, and on the first four validation images the centre-pixel MLP beat the patch CNN on both training losses (validation loss 2.145 against 2.241 on BP, 1.850 against 1.858 on ElasticNet) and on sparsity (1.90 against 1.96, BP 1.79). These ElasticNet runs used α = 1, the label-generation default, not the supervised side's α = 0.001 (Appendix B).

The test split and the mean (2 August). On the 153 test images the sparsity score and AIA MAE reproduced validation to the third decimal. The mean per-pixel BP loss proved unusable: the single worst pixel held 94.0% of the MLP's mean, which put that mean at four times the CNN's although the MLP was better at every percentile, so the BP loss has been reported by percentiles since. A census of 190,337 held-out pixels found 15.96% of BP DEMs bimodal (14.17% with both peaks interior); the MLP flagged interior-bimodal pixels at 80.75% precision and 29.85% recall.

The width sweep and the capacity ceiling (3 to 7 August). MLPs from 10k to 11.2M parameters, 40 epochs each. The sweep chose width 232 (176k parameters): eight times smaller than 1.43M at nearly the same DEM MAE (0.1266 against 0.1219) and a lower AIA MAE (4.792 against 4.898), while at width 160 the recall of bimodal pixels fell from 26.3% to 8.1%. Above width 232 recall stayed at 26% to 30% up to 11.2M. Re-solving BP under photon noise at 80 single-peaked and 80 double-peaked bright pixels (30 re-solves each) put the network's distance from BP at 0.69 and 0.98 times BP's own re-solve scatter, so most of the double-peak deficit was the label's irreproducibility. With fresh pixels (Appendix C) the recall cliff did not reproduce and width 336 beat 232 on nearly every test measure, so 336 became the width of both tracks' models at the time (section 5.4; the BP final later moved to 680, section 3.5); for the old model the self-consistency ratios are 0.97 at double-peaked and 0.70 at single-peaked pixels.

B. ElasticNet detail and the epochs trade

Objective and settings. The ElasticNet model trains on the solver's objective itself (section 3.2), with the supervised side's settings: scikit-learn's ElasticNet, non-negative, no intercept, α = 0.001, l1 ratio λ = 0.5 and C = 6, the number of channels. The same settings produced the supervised model's labels and every ElasticNet test target. The label-free ElasticNet runs of July and August used α = 1, the label-generation default; they are valid for their own objective but not comparable with the supervised side's solver, and no number in this report comes from them.

Input, width and epochs. The square root plus 12 Fourier frequencies input was chosen on validation (validation loss 0.0533 against 0.0575 for log1p) and lifted the 336-wide model past the supervised model on every measure (Table 5.2). The width and the number of epochs were settled with test evidence: with clamp pixels excluded, wider models blow up on a few rare pixels that the validation sample did not contain (sections 5.4 and 7.1). Keeping clamp pixels removes most of the 10M model's blow-up but costs the 409k model more than it gives (Table B.1), so the ElasticNet model excludes them.

Table B.1. ElasticNet follow-up runs on the shared test set; the first row repeats the ElasticNet model's numbers from Table 5.2.

ElasticNet run DEM MSE DEM MAE Median pixel error EM error W1 (dex) AIA MAE AIA MSE Flare-core emission Flare-core 94 Å
ElasticNet model (40 epochs) 0.310 0.151 0.85 12.2% 0.103 0.56 161 99% 53%
Oversample flare cores 0.379 0.152 0.89 12.2% 0.105 0.57 141 102% 55%
120 epochs 0.362 0.144 0.78 11.9% 0.100 0.52 188 102% 55%
10M parameters 2,062 0.159 0.78 15.2% 0.099 2.62 83M 216% 107%
Clamp pixels kept 0.439 0.201 1.55 17.0% 0.143 0.62 162 101% 54%
10M parameters, clamp pixels kept 1.82 0.198 1.48 17.2% 0.143 0.71 1.5 × 10⁵ 104% 56%

The epochs trade. 120 epochs improves five measures (DEM MAE 0.151 to 0.144, median pixel error 0.85 to 0.78, EM error 12.2% to 11.9%, W1 0.103 to 0.100, AIA MAE 0.56 to 0.52) and worsens two (DEM MSE 0.310 to 0.362, AIA MSE 161 to 188). The 40-epoch model was kept: DEM MSE is the one headline measure on which the supervised model comes close (0.318), and at 120 epochs the label-free model would lose it. That choice was made on the test set. Oversampling worsens DEM MSE (0.379) and changes little else; the 10M model blows up on a few rare pixels, as on BP. Clamp pixels in training cost the 409k model on most measures; the 10M model with them matches that run on DEM MAE, the median and W1, but has DEM MSE 1.82 and AIA MSE 1.5 × 10⁵.

Flare cores. Flare cores hold 44.5% of the ElasticNet model's DEM squared error (the supervised model's: 33.9%), but this is not the BP failure. The ElasticNet loss is the solver's objective itself, not a relaxation of it, so its best answer is the solver's own answer and there is no band to price. At flare cores the model reproduces the channels as the ElasticNet solver does, including the solver's own shortfall on 94 Å, which comes from its regularisation trading fit for smoothness.

Table B.2. ElasticNet flare cores on the shared test set (75,832 pixel-targets).

ElasticNet model Supervised Solver
Emission vs solver 99% 87% 100%
Peak height vs solver 101% 92% 100%
94 Å reproduced 53% 48% 55%
131 Å reproduced 80% 68% 78%
171 Å reproduced 97% 70% 100%
Curves with extra peaks 18% 18% 21%

C. The fixed-sample bug

What happened. Until 2026-10-02 every scaled run drew the same 512 pixels from each block in every epoch, because the draw was seeded by the block index alone (src/zarr_data.py). Training therefore saw one fixed sample of 58,688 blocks × 512 = 30M pixels, about 0.8% of the roughly 3.8 billion training pixels, 40 times over. The results stayed valid for what they measured (test matched validation to the third decimal), but rare pixels were under-sampled: those at 10 or more times the Bright cutoff, about 0.09% of pixels, were a fixed set of about 27,000.

The fix. --resample_pixels (commit 7067355, EpochResampler in src/zarr_data.py) offsets each epoch's indices so that every epoch draws fresh pixels; the first epoch's draw is unchanged, so default loaders behave as before (tests/test_zarr_data.py).

The first retrain came out worse. The width-232 models retrained with fresh pixels and otherwise identical settings scored worse than the fixed-sample ones by more than run-to-run noise (identical configurations agree to 0.2% to 0.4% in validation loss).

Table C.1. Width 232, fixed sample against fresh pixels, shared test set.

BP, fixed BP, fresh ElasticNet, fixed ElasticNet, fresh
Validation loss 2.156 2.237 0.0582 0.0689
DEM MSE 4.19 5.28 0.588 0.794
Median pixel error 0.026 0.030 1.41 1.70
Flare-core emission 41% 15% 72% 73%
Flare-core 94 Å 24% 7% 26% 40%
Flare-core curves with extra peaks 83% 89% 81% 40%

A plausible reason, untested: the objective is heavy-tailed, and a fixed sample lets the model absorb its pathological pixels once, while fresh pixels bring new ones every epoch, whose clipped gradients dominate the steps.

What it changed. The method trains on fresh pixels, so the report uses fresh-pixel models even though this first retrain scored worse. The width sweep and the CNN comparison were rerun with fresh pixels: width 336 beat 232 on nearly every test measure on both tracks (BP DEM MSE 4.28 against 5.28, median pixel error 0.026 against 0.030; ElasticNet DEM MSE 0.48 against 0.79), the recall cliff at width 160 did not reproduce, and the patch CNN still lost (section 5.4). Every scaled result dated 31 July to 28 September, including the September flare-core diagnosis, was measured on the fixed sample, and Appendix A labels it as history.

D. Reproducibility

Checkpoints. On the cluster, under output/experiments/ (not tracked in git):

  • Final BP model: output/experiments/followup/scaled_mlp6_barrier_h680_sqrt_ff12_resample_clampmask_mu100_ep120.pt.
  • ElasticNet model: input_encoding/scaled_mlp6_enet_h336_sqrt_ff12_resample.pt.
  • 409k stiff-band model: followup/scaled_mlp6_barrier_h336_sqrt_ff12_resample_mu100_ep120_cont.pt, warm-started from followup/scaled_mlp6_barrier_h336_sqrt_ff12_resample_mu100_ep120.pt.
  • Old model: resample/scaled_mlp6_barrier_h336_resample.pt.

The supervised models are in the repository, as supplied: eval_and_enet_specs/checkpoints/model_best_bp.pth and model_best_en.pth.

Data. Training and validation read the staged zarr stores $SCRATCH/dem/data/lp_AIA_hofdeconv_full_DS/ (BP) and $SCRATCH/dem/data/elasticnet_AIA_hofdeconv_full_DS/ (ElasticNet): per split, AIA in {phase}_x, the solver DEM in {phase}_y and the solver's tolerance level in {phase}_m. Training never reads {phase}_y; in the ElasticNet store it holds the older α = 1 labels and serves only validation diagnostics. Every test number comes from the supervised side's staged shared test set (48,960 blocks per track; its path is recorded in the data field of each diagnostic JSON), scored with the Bright thresholds in eval_and_enet_specs/aia_thresholds.json and the protocol in eval_and_enet_specs/README.md.

Scripts (names only). Label generation and staging: dataset/inv_bp_aia_hofdeconv_full.sh, eval_and_enet_specs/submit_enet_aia_hofdeconv_full.py, dataset/stage_hofdeconv_full.sh, dataset/job_stage_hofdeconv.sbatch. Training (experiments/train_scaled.py): experiments/job_scaled.sbatch, job_train_resample.sbatch, job_sweep_resample.sbatch, job_train_input_encoding.sbatch, job_train_enet_alpha0p001.sbatch, job_train_followup.sbatch (submitted by submit_followup.sh; the final BP model is its bp_h680_clampmask entry, width 680, μ = 100, 120 epochs, CLAMP_MODE=mask). Evaluation: job_eval_full_paper_test.sbatch, job_eval_supervised_paper_test.sbatch, job_diagnose_bright_failures.sbatch, job_aia_fit_by_brightness.sbatch, job_eval_followup_gpu.sbatch, job_eval_scaled.sbatch, job_eval_sweep.sbatch, job_objective_gap.sbatch. The October follow-ups of section 7 and section 8: job_mu_theory.sbatch, job_blowup_census.sbatch, job_jpdf_pixels.sbatch, job_final_layer.sbatch. Figures: experiments/plot_bright_failures.py --plain, with provenance in each results/plots/ folder's README.

Compute. GPU jobs stay under the cluster's 2-hour limit; longer runs are chains of resumable segments. An epoch of the 336-wide model takes about 150 s on one GPU, so 120 epochs is about 5 hours and 240 about 10; the final BP model took a median 169 s per epoch and 6.6 hours in all. The solvers took 9.5 min (BP) and 5.25 min (ElasticNet) per image in our July label-generation jobs. The network's inference time per image has not been measured, so the report claims no speed-up over the solvers.

Website. The viewer (code in student_package/visuals_pipeline/webapp/compare.html and compare.js; images built by experiments/job_visuals_final_cpu.sbatch) is public at https://triborough.cs.nyu.edu/hsr3649/demdemo/webapp/compare.html. Its code now shows the final BP model as run bp_mlp6_h680_clamp, with the self-check of section 7.1 blanking pixels whose DEM overshoots the observation by more than 100 times; the ElasticNet run is unchanged (enet_mlp6_h336_sqrtff). From 2026-10-19 the site showed the 409k stiff-band model (312 BP images), and an audit that day found all 1,875 build files byte-identical on the live site and all 72 numbers in its Results view matching the result JSONs; that audit has not been repeated for the new run. The server's TLS certificate expired on 2026-09-16, so browsers show a security warning; the warning concerns the server, not the viewer. The server was unreachable from 21 to 23 October and back on 24 October; a full copy of the site (6.5 GB) is kept off the server.
